chapters.question_prompt: When should I license my intellectual property rather than sell it, manufacture a product, or build a brand myself?
chapters.title: Choose the Licensing Business Model
chapters.subtitle: Licensing versus assignment, manufacturing and brand building; licensing fees, royalties, pure-play models and IP commercialization strategy
chapters.executive_summary: Patent attorneys, licensing coaches and product founders converge on one fork: make it yourself, sell the rights outright through an assignment, or license them while keeping title. Licensing wins the consensus for inventors who want the licensee's money, staff and shelf space. inventRightTV contrasts an instant 20,000-store footprint with the quarter-million-dollar inventory float that venturing demands. The street numbers are royalties of 2 to 10% of wholesale (Patent Question), 3 to 5% and up to 10% (Patent pc), 5 to 20% (UpCounsel), and roughly 7 to 11% in software (ICIP). Deal mechanics run from exclusive, co-exclusive and sole grants to field-of-use and territory splits, per-unit caps, guaranteed minimums and equity. The sharpest disagreement is over assignment. Some practitioners frame a lump sum as a clean exit. ICIP reports inventors asking a million dollars while buyers offer five thousand.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who maps the money starts from the same three-way fork. You can manufacture and sell the product yourself. You can sell the rights outright through an assignment. Or you can rent the rights out through a license while keeping title. Patent Question ranks manufacturing as the last of the three paths a new inventor should weigh, and calls it the most expensive and most time-consuming route because it drags in factories, inventory, packaging, shipping, customer service and returns [E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:00:31]. Eric Hanscom (ICIP) lays out the identical menu from the attorney's chair. Most inventors walk in wanting to make and sell it themselves for full control and full profit, then discover it becomes more than a full-time job for one person [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:00:22]. Michigan Engineering reduces the legal difference to real estate. An assignment is selling your house and a license is renting it. An exclusive license lets the tenant act like the owner while you still hold title [EPj0ydCGdiU @ 00:00:22]. UpCounsel adds the cash-flow trade. A sale delivers a quick one-time payout that can finance the next invention, but it forfeits every future dollar. Many inventors have sold patents for modest sums only to watch buyers generate substantial profits later [wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:00:48].

The consensus pick for an inventor who does not want to run a product company is licensing, and the reason is leverage on someone else's balance sheet. inventRightTV co-founders Stephen Key and Andrew boil it down to three benefits. The licensee invests its own money. Its sales, marketing, manufacturing and advertising people work for you. And you inherit its existing distribution: if the partner is already in 20,000 stores, your product lands in 20,000 stores [E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:02:07]. Key calls speed to market probably the best protection you can ever have, because a partner gets the product on the shelf faster than a solo founder who could take years while someone else jumps in [E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:02:40]. Patent Question lists the same borrowed assets: factory relationships, sales team, distribution channels, customer base, marketing budget and retail relationships. It says using them can save a huge amount of money and risk [E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:02:44]. Rich Goldstein's case file shows the payoff. One inventor patented a child safety product and licensed it to a major manufacturer that already had big-box shelf space, then collected royalties without ever worrying about production or distribution. A second inventor patented an idea with no strategy, and years later the patent expired without them making a dime [dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:02:24].

Practitioners agree that a license only works if there is something to rent. The Sourcing Gals draw the hard line. Another version of a tote bag with a great social following but nothing proprietary is very hard to license, because a partner could just make it themselves with no legal ramification. They also warn that design patents are hard to get unless the design is very utilitarian or functional. A utility patent, a strong design patent or a protected technology is what makes a product licensable [7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:14:50]. J.D. Houvener of Bold Patents says that to structure a contract around an asset you must own it, so yes, you need a patent to license. Know-how can be transferred under other contract types, but that is not a license [Vi4MIcyHOFE @ 00:08:44]. Houvener also says the patent does not have to be granted. A pending application backed by a reputable firm's search and legal opinion can itself be the licensed asset, and buyers may make an offer while it is still pending [Vi4MIcyHOFE @ 00:16:59]. Patent Question names the four things a serious company wants before it will evaluate a deal. The first is proof of concept from a prototype that may only prove function. The others are patent position, market fit, and business-focused pitch materials. The company is also asking whether it can proceed without you [E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:02:00].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The royalty numbers practitioners quote cluster low, and they depend on the base being measured. Rich Goldstein pegs inventor royalties at often 2 to 10% of wholesale sales, depending on the industry. In exchange, the inventor focuses on creating and protecting the invention while the company handles manufacturing, marketing and distribution [dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:00:43]. Patent pc gives a 3 to 5% range that can run as high as 10% of sales, granted on an exclusive or non-exclusive basis. Their outreach is to advertise the patent on licensing platforms or hit licensees directly through LinkedIn, Facebook, or an email from the company website [TYb3i3iIHEQ @ 00:00:45]. UpCounsel quotes a wider 5 to 20% band and draws the consequence: substantial profits require significant sales volume. In return, the licensee typically assumes liability for product mishaps, which cuts the inventor's risk [wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:02:12]. Eric Hanscom's session puts software licenses at roughly 7 to 11% on average and frames the real choice: Microsoft's or Apple's clout behind your marketing, or selling it yourself on eBay. The conclusion is blunt. They would rather take 1% of what Microsoft could do than ship packages out of their own garage [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:10:51].

The second lever is how much of the right you hand over, and practitioners slice it aggressively. Patent pc lays out three grants. An exclusive license gives one company the right, so you had better pick that partner very carefully. A non-exclusive license is the one to demand where you have market power, because it lets you license a number of players. A co-exclusive license goes to a specific group or number of licensees [A7xn_DzjKzE @ 00:01:21]. Kauffman FoundersSchool adds the sole license, where the licensor licenses only you but keeps the right to use the technology itself. It also covers field-of-use grants, where a licensee pays less for its own market segment while the licensor separately licenses unrelated fields to other partners [q5uDRlH_eFo @ 00:04:12]. Michigan Engineering slices by territory, with one licensee in the United States and another abroad. It also slices by industry, pharmaceutical to one party and biotech to another, and lets licensees sublicense those rights downstream [EPj0ydCGdiU @ 00:02:05]. J.D. Houvener pushes the slicing furthest. The rights to make, use, sell and import can be split, so one manufacturer is the only maker in the United States while a set of five to ten national retailers hold non-exclusive selling rights. Those retailers cannot make, use or import [Vi4MIcyHOFE @ 00:11:52].

Payment design is where the money is actually made or lost. Kauffman FoundersSchool walks the menu. There is a simple $1 per unit royalty. There is a one-time upfront payment, such as a million dollars and never another dime, for a permanent license. And there is a hybrid where per-unit royalties stop once a $1 million cap is reached and the license becomes permanent. Smaller licensees with near-term cash problems are told to push payments out as far as they can [q5uDRlH_eFo @ 00:06:08]. Michigan Engineering adds royalties on a percent of net sales and milestone fees triggered at set unit volumes. It also covers annual minimums that pressure the licensee to keep selling, and equity in place of cash when an early-stage licensee lacks the money [EPj0ydCGdiU @ 00:03:03]. Cashix describes the brand-side version, the guaranteed minimum royalty, a non-refundable floor paid regardless of units sold. It forces the manufacturing partner to carry the financial risk and stops competitors from buying licenses just to keep products off shelves [2dvDoXcllAw @ 00:01:40]. Patent Question insists the fine print moves real money. Gross versus net royalties, per-unit versus percentage, minimum quarterly payments versus none, exclusive versus non-exclusive, and reporting obligations all have to be pinned down when the deal is made [E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:04:13].

callout.title: Moves the operators use to get the deal and keep leverage
callout.body: Small positioning and timing choices change who calls back and what they pay.
items: Approach manufacturers as a product developer, not an inventor, using polished brochures, formal letters and prototypes. If you use a patent broker, never pay upfront fees, and vet the broker through the United Inventors Association and the Better Business Bureau first [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:03:31].

Expect price to be settled last, because every other term moves it. Your technology is worth no more than the cost of the licensee's next best alternative, and the quarter-to-a-third-of-profits rule of thumb is a starting point, not something to rely on [Kauffman FoundersSchool — q5uDRlH_eFo @ 00:01:41].

Retailers do not like dealing with one-SKU, one-product companies. Licensing into a partner that already has 15 products in Lowe's and more in Walmart gets your item through doors a solo launch cannot open [inventRightTV — E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:02:22].

Use licensing to hit adjacent markets at once. In medical technology, license into both the human and pet markets simultaneously instead of leaving one open for a competitor with similar technology [Licensing Consulting Group — 0MpPL7OXNr4 @ 00:01:22].

sop_steps.title: Test licensability before spending
sop_steps.action: Confirm the invention offers new features with a concrete benefit and has something proprietary to protect.
sop_steps.detail: Inventions that add new features and deliver benefits such as cost savings or performance improvement are the ones industry players will license. Research the target customer, competitors and industry trends before outreach [Patent pc — A7xn_DzjKzE @ 00:01:44]. If nothing about the product is proprietary, partners can copy it without paying [The Sourcing Gals — 7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:14:50].

sop_steps.title: Lock the asset cheaply
sop_steps.action: File a provisional to get patent-pending status and use NDAs in every partner conversation.
sop_steps.detail: A provisional application gives 12 months of patent-pending status while you explore commercialization [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:04:04]. inventRightTV says you can often spend less than $100 or $200 on a provisional, a sell sheet and a prototype, then potentially earn tens of thousands to $200,000 a year in royalties [inventRightTV — E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:06:33].

sop_steps.title: Build the package and work the channels
sop_steps.action: Assemble a licensing package, then reach licensees, retailers and brokers directly and persistently.
sop_steps.detail: Include a brief business plan, technical specifications, test data and a working prototype where possible [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:02:27]. Add manufacturing cost and product benefits, then reach buyers via LinkedIn, trade shows, the US Patent Office licensing listing, IP marketplaces and patent brokers, following up until someone orders [Patent pc — A7xn_DzjKzE @ 00:03:09].

sop_steps.title: Pin down the term sheet
sop_steps.action: Choose the grant type, then lock minimums, audit rights, duration and payment base in writing.
sop_steps.detail: Pick exclusive, non-exclusive or cross-licensing, then define minimum sales thresholds, audit rights and license duration. Have counsel draft scope, field of use, payment structure, sublicensing and termination clauses [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:02:59]. Specify gross versus net, per-unit versus percentage, and quarterly minimums [Patent Question — E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:04:13].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is over whether to build the product at all. Eric Hanscom (ICIP) reports that inventors walk in wanting to make and sell it themselves for complete control and all the profit, rank assignment second, and treat licensing as the third most attractive option, yet usually end up there because they lack the money to fund everything and nobody will pay what they think the invention is worth [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:06:40]. Stephen Key and Andrew of inventRightTV flip that ranking: licensing is 'way sexier' than vulture capital, Kickstarter, Indiegogo, or Shark Tank because a large company that likes the product will invest unlimited money in it [E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:01:14]. Rich Goldstein of Patent Question concedes the build-your-own-company path carries the highest potential upside but also takes the most effort, paying off in control and the ability to charge premium prices [dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:01:44]. The Sourcing Gals split the difference: pitching licensing straight out of the gate makes validation hard, so going to market first may still be the necessary proof-of-concept step, with licensing layered on later as a pivot or add-on that never has to replace the core business [7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:09:36].

Nobody agrees on what a royalty should be. Rich Goldstein of Patent Question pegs licensing royalties at often 2 to 10 percent of wholesale sales, depending on the industry, with the company handling manufacturing, marketing, and distribution [dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:00:43]. Patent pc calls licensing for recurring royalties the preferred path for most inventors and quotes a range anywhere between 3 to 5 percent or even as high as 10 percent of sales [TYb3i3iIHEQ @ 00:00:45]. UpCounsel stretches the band to 5 to 20 percent and warns that substantial profits therefore require significant sales volume, because licensing success depends on product performance in the market [wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:02:12]. In the ICIP session with Eric Hanscom, software licenses are put at roughly 7 to 11 percent on average, and the room concludes it would rather take 1 percent of what Microsoft could do than hassle with selling out of eBay with packages piled in the garage [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:10:51]. That line is the real argument hiding under every percentage quoted: a thin slice of a giant distribution machine can outrun a fat margin on tiny volume. The spread itself is the operator lesson, so benchmark against your own industry rather than a universal rate.

Selling versus renting the rights splits the room again. UpCounsel concedes that a sale delivers a quick one-time payout but warns that many inventors have sold patents for modest sums only to watch buyers generate substantial profits later, which is why it calls licensing the more profitable path for many inventors [wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:00:48]. Eric Hanscom (ICIP) explains why sales stall: an inventor asks a million dollars, the prospective buyer replies that the inventor has never sold one and the buyer still has to set up the factory, packaging, and marketing, then offers five thousand, so assignments usually do not go through easily and, when they do, both sides make major concessions [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:05:39]. Exclusivity is just as contested. Patent pc says that where you have market power you may want to demand non-exclusive licensing so you can license to a number of people, with co-exclusive grants to a specific group as a middle option, and warns an exclusive deal means picking your partner very carefully [A7xn_DzjKzE @ 00:01:04]. The Sourcing Gals push the opposite play: give one brand exclusive access for a certain period to potentially create bidding wars and amp up the deal [7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:13:58].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most detailed firsthand wound comes from inventRightTV. Stephen Key started the Hot Picks guitar-pick business, which became a Disney licensee, with $200,000 from friends and still came up short of money, even though the picks cost only two to three cents each to make [E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:04:47]. Once Walmart, Target, and 7-Eleven ordered, the company had to float at least a quarter of a million dollars to fill the pipeline while retailers took 60 to 90 days to pay and suppliers yelled to be paid; it ordered several runs ahead just to hit the schedule, and the founders stopped being creative because the job became managing inventory flow [E5dH32uMqOY @ 00:05:21]. Eric Hanscom (ICIP) maps the same grind from the factory floor: Chinese factories want at least a third paid up front, fast boats now take about three weeks and slow boats over a month, and large retailers fine you for barcode, carton-count, and late-delivery mistakes [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:04:06]. Patent Question draws the hard line: do not manufacture because someone called it a million-dollar idea, without tested demand, or without understanding your costs, and only consider it with strong demand, healthy margins, a clear sales channel, and the ability to manage operations [E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:05:11].

Licensing does not erase risk; it relocates it into oversight. Cashix lays out the naked-licensing trap: license a brand to a third party without strict, active quality control over the resulting products and a court can declare the trademark abandoned, so the primary commercial asset ceases to exist; the same breakdown warns licensors are exposed to the public behavior of volatile celebrity or erratic licensee partners [2dvDoXcllAw @ 00:03:54]. J.D. Houvener of Bold Patents says licenses are only as good as the job you do enforcing them, pointing to the firm's own license with a similarly named law firm in another state that is worthless unless the firm checks it stays inside the four corners of the contract [Vi4MIcyHOFE @ 00:12:38]. Co-host Matt adds the trademark version: know about an encroaching name but wait maybe five years before sending a cease and desist, and the other side can claim it already owns the brand because you led it to believe the use was okay [Vi4MIcyHOFE @ 00:07:46]. Rich Goldstein of Patent Question names the quietest failure of all: an inventor patented an idea with no strategy, and years went by until the patent expired without ever making a dime [dlTT-hWgkB8 @ 00:02:38].

The last trap set lives in the paperwork. Kauffman FoundersSchool tells licensees on fixed-term deals to get the license long enough to cover the entire need, because once the technology is baked into the platform the licensor knows it and the price of poker may go way up at renegotiation; the same session insists on exquisite attention to the final written agreement, down to comma placement [q5uDRlH_eFo @ 00:05:16]. Michigan Engineering lists the clauses that bite later: who owns improvements made while the licensee uses the technology, who controls ongoing patent prosecution, who is liable if someone is hurt, how long the license lasts, and what rights each side has to terminate if the deal stops paying off the way they anticipated [EPj0ydCGdiU @ 00:03:58]. Eric Hanscom (ICIP) gives the assignment version: leave filing decisions to the assignee and they may insist on a surfboard patent in Mongolia and take the cost off the net profits, so the inventor gets less [yUPS-UISPnQ @ 00:09:50]. UpCounsel adds the broker trap: patent brokers market inventions for a commission on sales, so never pay upfront fees and check reputation through the United Inventors Association and Better Business Bureau before proceeding [wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:03:48].

callout.title: Kill-Switch Checks Before You Lock In a Path
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, reversal, or bottleneck the practitioners hit or watched others hit. Fail any one and the chosen path is not ready.
items: No proprietary, protectable element locked in means no licensing pitch; The Sourcing Gals refuse further deal conversations until the technology is protected [The Sourcing Gals — 7aTTgSE0elA @ 00:24:41].
No manufacturing without strong demand, healthy margins, a clear sales channel, and the ability to manage operations [Patent Question — E7nUaZBoVeI @ 00:05:27].
No broker paid upfront fees; brokers work on commission and get checked through the United Inventors Association and Better Business Bureau [UpCounsel — wiI7fBL42Vg @ 00:03:48].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I research patents, trace ownership, consider provisional protection and decide what professional help I need before licensing an invention?
chapters.title: Research and Protect the Invention
chapters.subtitle: USPTO searches, application numbers, design searches, assignment records, provisional filing, licensing without patents and patent-practice boundaries
chapters.executive_summary: Licensing practitioners converge on a lean protection stack: research first, file a provisional for perceived ownership, and keep title before licensing rights out. inventRightTV reports 99% of its students over 15 years licensed without a patent, uses $65 micro-entity provisionals, and pushes the licensee to fund the non-provisional, with a 7/5/1 tiered royalty. John Ferrell insists on knowing your price, refusing permanent assignment, and enforcing annual minimums. On the research side, Edel Patents and USPTO examiner Edward teach concept-based Boolean searching where parentheses alone cut one example from 316 hits to 46, plus traps around leading zeros, legacy syntax, and application numbers. Adam Diament and Patents Demystified mine assignment records for owners, collateral, and licensing contacts. The split: Edel dismisses Quick Search that Erinnae Baker teaches, while inventRightTV's Andrew hedges on going fully patent-free.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the licensing camp the baseline is blunt: an issued patent is not the entry ticket. inventRightTV states that 99% of the students taught over the last 15 years licensed product ideas without a patent [CS31715RNQk @ 00:01:31], and the same channel says flatly that you do not need a patent to license an idea, because companies will not defend one in federal court and 'you're not going to sue everybody' [fyUYT-gfzfU @ 00:00:36]. What replaces the patent, in the same camp's words, is perceived ownership, built with a provisional patent application that buys one year of patent-pending status. The USPTO's own outreach talk confirms the mechanics behind that strategy: a provisional lasts 12 months and is never examined [binARAl4AK8 @ 00:28:18]. John Ferrell frames the same discipline from the deal side, insisting you never pursue a patent without a business reason and that you walk into any manufacturer meeting already knowing your price, or you end up inside someone else's agenda [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:01:28]. The common thread is that protection is a commercial lever, sized to the deal, rather than a trophy filed for its own sake before any company has shown interest.

The second point of agreement is that research comes before filing, and that it starts cheap. inventRightTV's first requirement is a genuinely new idea, checked against Google Image and Google Shopping until a clear point of difference shows up [fyUYT-gfzfU @ 00:01:25]. Erinnae Baker positions the USPTO database for exactly the same job: pulling technical specs, seeing whether an idea has already been done, and judging how similar existing patents are, with full text running from 1976 and partial data reaching back to 1790 [Awpsichbouw @ 00:02:37]. Edel Patents adds the mindset that separates a useful search from a wasted afternoon: 'search for the concept not the word,' because the document you need 'lies at the intersection of a few concepts' [SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:03:09]. Intellectual Property Ontario's analyst Dilshay Singh draws the same line between modes, reserving basic search for known items, names and dates, and pushing anything conceptual into the advanced command-line syntax documented under the Help tab [2L5qDLM_EkY @ 00:02:30]. Put together, the practitioners treat search as the cheapest insurance in the whole chain: it tells you whether a point of difference exists before a single dollar goes into a provisional or a pitch.

The third consensus is about who actually owns the asset you are about to license. Patents Demystified starts from the default: inventors own the rights in a patent or application, with no work-for-hire rule like copyright, so ownership only moves through employment, partnership or collaboration agreements [zel57Kej5nY @ 00:01:05]. Idea2PatentAI repeats that rights initially belong to the inventors and treats recording an inventor assignment through Assignment Center as the optional last step of a provisional filing [ixENhsfAdEA @ 00:05:52]. Adam Diament explains why that optional step matters: recording is technically optional but highly recommended, because the first party to record usually wins a dispute, and unrecorded company assignments create headaches during fundraising and acquisitions [k0S01jxvk6M @ 00:03:00]. John Ferrell closes the loop on the licensing side with a hard rule against permanently assigning patents, copyrights, trademarks or trade secrets to a manufacturer, since a bankrupt licensee would then own your rights; an exclusive license, he says, is fine [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:02:24]. The operator takeaway is consistent across all four: know exactly whose name sits on title, record every transfer you make, and license rights out rather than selling them.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the search engine itself, the mechanics get specific. Edel Patents tells beginners to skip Quick Search entirely, build each concept from OR-joined synonyms, stack concepts with AND so that every AND shortens the list, wrap niche phrases in quotes, and lean on grouping because 'the search engine really likes parentheses' [SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:04:08]. USPTO examiner Edward puts a number on that advice: the same dog-and-bowl example returns 316 hits without parentheses and 46 with them [np8RKbVMSLg @ 00:23:30]. In Patent Public Search Advanced the index sits at the end wrapped in periods, as in (dog and bowl).TI., legacy syntax will not retrieve accurate results, and document-number fields need seven characters, so you pad with leading zeros because the PN button will not add them for you [np8RKbVMSLg @ 00:14:03]. Edward's design-only filters, S.AT. or S.KD., each cut his example down to 31 hits, and date windows run in formats such as @AY>=2014. Dilshay Singh of Intellectual Property Ontario works the same grammar from the analyst side, using .ab. for abstract, .as. for assignee, @pd>= for a date range, NEAR n for bidirectional proximity and * as a wildcard [2L5qDLM_EkY @ 00:03:34].

Finding a specific application is its own minefield. Edel Patents breaks the number into a two-digit series code plus a six-digit serial written as 2 digits, slash, 3 digits, comma, 3 digits, and warns that the filing receipt carries two eight-digit numbers at the top, so grabbing the wrong one means 'looking for a patent application that doesn't exist' [oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:01:47]. The USPTO search rejects full application numbers outright, so his reliable path runs from the USPTO site to Patents, Find It Fast and Public PAIR, adding a slash after the first two digits if it fails and simply retrying on errors; PatentScope is fast, while Google Patents is fast but fails more often [oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:06:09]. Once inside, the Image File Wrapper holds the prosecution history, and the move he singles out is comparing claim 1 of the pre-grant publication against the granted claim, highlighting the added language, because 'there's a really good chance you just ran your highlighter over one of the most important weaknesses in the patent' [oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:07:21]. Adam Diament notes provisionals are harder still, requiring the application number to surface at all [k0S01jxvk6M @ 00:06:58].

The filing and deal numbers are where the economics land. Idea2PatentAI says the provisional upload itself takes under 30 minutes in Patent Center, using a free USPTO account with identity verification, the specification, drawings, an Application Data Sheet it calls the most important form, and a micro entity certification, with fees paid the same day: $130 small or $65 micro, on Eastern time [ixENhsfAdEA @ 00:05:22]. The USPTO's Marilyn Nash lists the full ladder: provisional fees of $325 large, $130 small and $65 micro, nonprovisional fees of $400 to $2,000, and attorney fees of roughly $6,000 to $18,000 [binARAl4AK8 @ 00:29:33]. inventRightTV prices a full patent at about $15k against products that mostly sell for 2 to 3 years while examination runs 1.5 to 4 years, then hands over the contract mechanics: open up the grant of license to fold in improvements, keep filing new provisionals to stay patent pending, and tier the royalty at 7% if granted, 5% if pending and 1% if it never issues [CS31715RNQk @ 00:11:10]. John Ferrell's example royalty is 5 cents per widget, backed by an annual minimum that ends the contract and returns all rights to the inventor if missed [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:03:02].

callout.title: Search and Ownership Edges Most Inventors Miss

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to pay for a patent before pitching. inventRightTV goes all-in on no: Stephen reports that 99% of the students Stephen and Andrew taught over 15 years licensed without a patent [CS31715RNQk @ 00:01:31], and after defending six-plus patents against a toy company in federal court concluded that patents are just words. The replacement is perceived ownership through a provisional, with the licensee negotiated into paying for the expensive non-provisional [fyUYT-gfzfU @ 00:03:13]. Even inside that camp the line bends: Andrew hedges with I wouldn't say no when asked whether patents matter, and big ideas still demand a wall of patents. John Ferrell, Esq. frames the question as a business test rather than a creed, opening with the rule that nobody should get a patent without a business reason [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:00:00]. Marilyn Nash of USPTOvideo puts numbers on what both camps are reacting to: provisional fees of $325 large, $130 small and $65 micro, nonprovisional fees of $400 to $2,000, and attorney fees running about $6,000 to $18,000 [binARAl4AK8 @ 00:29:33]. inventRightTV's own dividing line holds: small consumer products that sell for two to three years ride a provisional and shelf space, while big ideas justify the full patent wall.

Search-tool advice splits just as hard. Erinnae Baker walks beginners through Quick Search with Boolean pairs like bicycle AND speedometer and speedometer NOT automobile, and warns that the advanced search is pretty difficult to use [Awpsichbouw @ 00:02:56]. Edel Patents rejects that starting point outright: Quick Search rarely works for patent searching and is not worth your time, so build every query in Advanced Search around concepts made of OR-joined synonyms, wrapped in parentheses and joined by AND [SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:00:18]. Dilshay Singh of Intellectual Property Ontario splits the difference, keeping basic search for known items, names and dates, as in assignee Apple AND inventor jobs returning 617 records, and reserving the command-line advanced mode for concept work such as disc brakes from five named assignees published 2015 to 2022 [2L5qDLM_EkY @ 00:00:39]. On speed versus reliability for pulling a known application, Edel Patents prefers Public PAIR and flags that Google Patents is very fast but unsuccessful more often [oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:06:09], while Patents Demystified builds its whole ownership-history workflow inside Google Patents through Application events, Show all events and the USPTO assignment link. Edel Patents boils it down: fast is only great if it works.

Ownership transfer is where the deal camps diverge. John Ferrell, Esq. treats a permanent assignment of patents, copyrights, trademarks or trade secrets as a rookie mistake, because if the manufacturer goes bankrupt it owns your rights, so license them, exclusively if needed, and never transfer outright [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:02:24]. Patents Demystified starts from the opposite direction: inventors own by default, there is no work-for-hire rule as with copyright, so companies pull rights in through employment, partnership and collaboration agreements and then record them to perfect title like a county deed [zel57Kej5nY @ 00:01:36]. Idea2PatentAI lists recording an inventor assignment through Assignment Center as an optional sixth step after a provisional filing, and Adam Diament calls recording technically optional but highly recommended because the first to record usually wins disputes [k0S01jxvk6M @ 00:03:00]. On royalty structure, inventRightTV skips the fight over whether a patent will ever issue by tiering the payout: seven if granted, five if pending, one if it never issues, while opening the grant of license so new improvements and fresh provisionals keep the inventor patent pending [CS31715RNQk @ 00:11:10]. Ferrell goes further, keeping every improvement, whether suggested by the manufacturer or a customer, with the inventor and insisting the contract be written by a lawyer in the inventor's state rather than pulled from an internet template.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest mistakes happen at the negotiating table. John Ferrell, Esq. describes the buyer who asks the price and gets silence, which signals you are not ready to talk; walk in without a number and you become part of someone else's agenda [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:01:28]. Ferrell's other traps compound: no annual minimum, leaving a 5-cents-per-widget deal without the clause that ends the contract and sends the rights back to you [Te8GX-Xx4mo @ 00:03:02], and indemnifying the manufacturer for products liability, manufacturing mistakes, late delivery or advertising fraud. Ferrell's rule is blunt: never indemnify the manufacturer. inventRightTV flags industry selection as a silent killer: the tech industry is a terrible industry where those guys don't play fair, and packaging, the speaker's own industry, is just hard, while toy, pet, kitchen and hardware stay open [fyUYT-gfzfU @ 00:02:03]. The litigation path carries its own scar tissue. Stephen defended six-plus patents in federal court against a toy company and walked away convinced patents are just words, the root of the no-patent playbook [CS31715RNQk @ 00:06:32]. Ferrell's final gate is relational: perception is reality, and if a partner does not feel right, back away before anything is signed.

Research failures burn days instead of dollars. Edel Patents warns that the filing receipt carries two eight-digit numbers, and grabbing the wrong one means hunting for an application that doesn't exist, while the USPTO search rejects full application numbers outright [oOln2IDvhqE @ 00:01:47]. Examiner Edward of USPTOvideo stacks more syntax traps: legacy format no longer retrieves accurate results, document and patent number fields need seven characters padded with leading zeros, the PN button will not add those zeros for you, and dropping parentheses turned a 46-hit query into 316 [np8RKbVMSLg @ 00:15:25]. Sessions carry no accounts and the workspace cannot be saved, with a 30-minute idle timeout, a 2-minute warning and a 5-minute grace period. Edel Patents adds that abstract searches narrow so quickly you can lose important documents [SDXhhmDKGJo @ 00:04:28]. Ownership data has its own blind spots. Adam Diament notes that errors recorded in the assignment database last forever, down to a missing comma in Cool Startup, Inc., that many licenses are private and never recorded, and that unrecorded company assignments cause headaches in fundraising and acquisitions [k0S01jxvk6M @ 00:05:38]. Examiner Edward also warns that the assignee printed on a patent is current only as of its issue date.

Filing and practice traps close the loop. Idea2PatentAI stresses that a provisional only protects what it discloses, so leaving out implementation details can impact your rights, and filing fees of $130 small or $65 micro must be paid the same day on Eastern time [ixENhsfAdEA @ 00:05:22]. Marilyn Nash of USPTOvideo resets expectations on timeline and enforcement: office action rejections are normal, first action takes 24 to 36 months unless Track 1 compresses disposition to about 12, and the USPTO is not an enforcement agency [binARAl4AK8 @ 00:35:34]. For anyone running research or filings as a service, Jim Selbach treats unauthorized practice of law as both an ethical violation and a crime, notes that exercising independent judgment counts as advice, and cites a PI lawyer who lost a license over paralegal settlements [0r9cstgrqZM @ 00:06:42]. Patents Demystified passed the patent bar in the first semester of law school and built a solo firm off referrals, then watched a merged downtown firm dissolve over attorney non-attorney profit sharing issues [GOd61uYqq-8 @ 00:01:28]. Berkeley Center for Law & Technology panelists add a retention signal: Adam Cole recommends two-plus years as an agent before law school, and one hire quit after about a year and a half.

chapters.question_prompt: What can inventors actually earn from licensing, and how should I assess royalty expectations against manufacturing and other monetization options?
chapters.title: Understand Inventor Royalty Economics
chapters.subtitle: Royalty-percentage negotiation, licensing versus manufacturing, Stephen Key's product earnings, Brian Walker's royalty story and practical patent monetization
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree that licensing means renting your rights to a company that already owns manufacturing and distribution, then collecting royalties without running a business. The rate band is tight. UpCounsel cites 3 to 6% of gross sales. Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss see about 5% most often, seven or eight when CAD, testing, or tooling is done, and over 10% only for Disney-level brands. The street mechanics are cheap: a $25 Kinko's prototype produced a contract in three days and $100,000 in first-year royalties, a three-hour toy built from shop parts generated about $10 million, and Key files provisional applications for $65. They split on tactics. Sef Chang lets the company crunch its numbers before naming a percentage. J.D. Houvener walks in with written walk-away terms. Jeff Schell trades royalty points for licensee-funded enforcement.

key_metrics.label: Most Common Consumer-Product Royalty Rate
key_metrics.context: Key and Krauss call 5% the most common average they have seen across years of student licensing deals. They say it drops toward three for high-volume consumables and climbs to seven or eight when the inventor has done CAD, testing, or tooling.

key_metrics.label: Typical Patent Royalty Range
key_metrics.context: UpCounsel's average range for patent royalty rates, which varies with industry, the uniqueness of the invention, and patent strength.

key_metrics.label: Light Chaser Lifetime Royalties
key_metrics.value: About $10 million, one third to the agent
key_metrics.context: Brian Walker's three-hour, zero-cost toy prototype, licensed to SRM Entertainment. Walker estimates it sold seven to eight hundred million dollars at retail.

key_metrics.label: Spin Label Annual Minimum Guarantees
key_metrics.context: Key's rotating label paid royalties off and on for roughly 20 years. Minimum guarantees ranged from a quarter million dollars in some years to $750,000 in others.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner in this lane describes the same core trade: the inventor keeps the idea and rents the rights to a company that already owns manufacturing and distribution. Brian Fried has collected royalty checks for over 18 years. Fried first pushes an idea through a search, a patentability opinion, a prototype, and 3-D CAD. Then the intellectual property goes to a company that will manufacture it, sell it through internal or third-party sales reps, and pay a royalty [UnGdjQb467o @ 00:00:59]. Patent attorney Jeff Schell frames the same deal as a permission grant in exchange for a fee or royalty. Schell calls it a win-win, because the licensee gets to sell the patented invention legally [cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:00:33]. J.D. Houvener explains why the model beats building a company for most inventors. Raising money, hiring employees, taking manufacturing risk, selling to strangers, and carrying HR paperwork is a ton of effort, and many inventors already have full-time jobs and children [2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:03:23]. Stephen Key pushes the risk point hardest: there is no financial risk and you do not have to quit your day job. Key's wife Janice took a full-time job for the health insurance while Key learned to license, and the family moved from simple ideas to big ones that built a large revenue stream [hbfKyomYp6U @ 00:02:59].

On the headline number, the speakers cluster tightly in the low single digits. UpCounsel puts typical patent royalty rates at 3 to 6% of gross sales. The rate swings with industry, the uniqueness of the invention, and the strength of the patent [mtxmo_OkhSw @ 00:00:30]. Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss have coached students for years. They peg the most common consumer-product rate at about 5% and drop it toward three for huge-volume consumables. The rate climbs to seven or eight when the inventor has already done CAD drawings, testing, a prototype, or even tooling. They also warn that over 10% is Disney territory, citing a secondhand report of a 20% rate on The Lion King at its peak [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:05:09]. Sef Chang, interviewed by The Patent Professor, gives a generic range of one or two up to five percent. Chang acknowledges that some licensors land 14, 15, or 20, but says the companies themselves often do not know the right number until they do the math [bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:00:20]. Brian Fried specifies the base: the royalty is typically a percentage of the wholesale price the licensee charges the retail buyer. Fried is paid quarterly and gets sell-through reports showing units sold by store and by product variation [UnGdjQb467o @ 00:01:58]. Double digits show up on the record only as outliers or big-brand deals. The practitioners never treat them as the opening position for an independent inventor.

The bigger consensus is that the rate alone is a vanity number. Krauss argues that a half-percent royalty on a bazillion units can beat a fat rate on thin volume. Krauss adds that 5% on half a million units a year may be extremely generous. Key's formula has three inputs: volume, royalty rate, and price point, whether the product sells for $500, $19, or 99 cents. Key runs all three through a calculator before signing anything [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:07:09]. Exclusivity is the second lever everyone names. Schell ranks the payouts this way. Exclusive licenses usually return the highest royalties. Sole licenses sit in the middle, because the inventor keeps the right to use the invention. Non-exclusive deals pay less per licensee but let multiple payers stack [cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:01:08]. Houvener calls the exclusive versus non-exclusive choice a huge price negotiation. Houvener also stresses that the license term is rarely the full twenty-year patent life, because both sides want to return to the table if the market takes off or stalls [ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:04:12]. The third shared truth is patience. Key says money does not start at signing. The company must make the product, ship it, and get it on the shelf, and then distribution has to grow. Royalties really add up after a year, a year and a half, or two years [Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:06:40]. Operators who need cash next quarter should keep a day job funding the pipeline.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Key's street method is to spend almost nothing until a company says yes. For the Michael Jordan Wall Ball, Key made the prototype at Kinko's using a $15 Ohio Art backboard and a $10 poster, roughly $25 total. Key had a licensing agreement three days later, and the product earned about $100,000 in first-year royalties and sold for 10 years [gxeuCPaGeHY @ 00:04:08]. The Sweet Darts arrow needed no prototype and no intellectual property filing at all. It paid about $10,000 for one Valentine's season and never sold again [Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:02:53]. Brian Walker built the original Light Chaser in three hours from parts already sitting in the shop. Walker assumed the $5,000 advance would be the only money ever seen. Instead the toy reached an estimated seven to eight hundred million dollars at retail across more than a hundred versions [WEVVJ111b8o @ 00:04:13]. Key's current cost stack is even lower. An AI prototype costs nothing, and 3D printing lets you Frankenstein a model together. Key uses AI to write a provisional patent application and file it at the USPTO for $65 [hM7gpPqIDoQ @ 00:17:40]. The workhorse tool is the sell sheet, a one-page advertisement that sells the benefit. Key uses it to gauge company interest before any real money moves on prototypes or patents.

In the negotiation room, Sef Chang refuses to name a percentage first. Chang asks only whether the company is interested. The company then calls manufacturers, gets quotes, and crunches its own profit. Next Chang asks for the cost rundown and moves the needle back and forth. If the percentage lands low, Chang negotiates for something else that compensates [bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:01:06]. Krauss names those other levers. If the company offers three but you wanted four, push the minimum guarantees higher. Require guaranteed sales figures with the rights coming back if they are missed, or have the company pay for your patents [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:03:20]. Houvener tells inventors to walk in with two plans: the perfect deal and the walk-away terms, such as at least four percent royalty or an exclusive grant. Holding those terms in hand gives you posture and keeps you professional instead of emotional [ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:02:26]. Schell offers a trade most rookies miss. Under an exclusive arrangement, accept slightly lower royalties in exchange for putting the expensive obligation to enforce the patent on the licensee [cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:02:52]. Houvener also carves deals surgically. One option is licensing claims one through ten to one party and claims eleven through twenty to another. Another is splitting make and sell rights across Canada, the US, and Mexico.

The unit math is simple and brutal. Key's chart starts with the number of stores the licensee is in. Assume each store sells one unit a week, because anything slower gets kicked to the curb. Then run the result at 3, 4, 5, and 6% across chains like Walmart, Target, Lowe's, and Home Depot [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:02:17]. Krauss contrasts the do-it-yourself alternative. You could sell 5,000 to 20,000 units yourself at a 20% profit margin while working 60 to 80 hour weeks. Or a licensee could move half a million units a year while you do no work [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:04:09]. At the top end, Key's rotating label paid royalties for over 15 years and made about $10 million. It ran on Nescafe, Jim Beam, and Lawry's, with sublicenses in Japan and Ireland [hM7gpPqIDoQ @ 00:13:06]. Walker's Light Chaser checks climbed from $75,000 to $180,000, $260,000, and $340,000 in the breakout year. Later checks reached $250,000 to $350,000 per quarter, but a third of roughly $10 million went to an agent [WEVVJ111b8o @ 00:05:41]. Splits cut the take too. The Wall Ball was a split royalty, with partner Russell Hicks taking half. Its final check, for 53 cents, was never cashed.

callout.title: How the pros squeeze more out of every royalty deal
callout.body: These are moves the practitioners actually run at the table and before it, so the rate, the guarantees, and the rights all tilt toward the inventor.
items: Never open with a percentage. Let the company get manufacturer quotes and crunch its own profit, then move the needle from its numbers [The Patent Professor — bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:00:38]
Interview the licensee about volume before signing. If the numbers are small and nobody else is interested, grant a non-exclusive instead of an exclusive [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:07:53]
Under an exclusive deal, trade slightly lower royalties for making the licensee carry the expensive job of enforcing the patent [Jeff Schell — cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:02:52]

sop_steps.title: Validate with a sell sheet before spending
sop_steps.action: Build a one-page advertisement selling the benefit and send it to target companies before any prototype or patent spend.
sop_steps.detail: Gauge interest first, and build a prototype only when a company wants proof of concept, because prototyping every idea burns too much time and money [inventRightTV — INuH7fr5H40 @ 00:04:26]

sop_steps.title: File a well-written provisional application
sop_steps.action: Draft and file a provisional patent application that includes manufacturing notes, workarounds, variations, materials, and good drawings.
sop_steps.detail: A provisional with enough detail to show how the product could be made carries value with companies, and it costs far less than filing full patents on every idea [inventRightTV — INuH7fr5H40 @ 00:07:33]

sop_steps.title: Run the royalty math on the licensee
sop_steps.action: Multiply projected annual units by price point by royalty rate, and test 3% through 6% against the licensee's real store count.
sop_steps.detail: Get a calculator out and model the units at that price and rate. The numbers may reveal that the licensee lacks the volume to be worth an exclusive [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:07:23]

sop_steps.title: Negotiate from a written walk-away list
sop_steps.action: Enter the meeting with your perfect-deal terms and your deal breakers written down. Then trade on minimum guarantees, term, territory, and enforcement.
sop_steps.detail: Having goals and walk-away terms in hand gives you posture and keeps you professional and unemotional across the negotiation [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:02:26]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The number everyone wants is the royalty rate, and the operators do not quote the same one. UpCounsel pins the average at 3 to 6% of gross sales, with the figure moving on industry, uniqueness of the invention and strength of the patent [mtxmo_OkhSw @ 00:00:30]. Sef Chang, interviewed on The Patent Professor, gives a lower generic band of two percent, maybe even one, up to five, while noting that some people have landed 14, 15 or 20 and warning that even the companies themselves do not really know the right number until they do the math [bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:00:20]. Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss at inventRightTV call about 5% the most common rate they see, drop high-volume consumables toward three, push it to seven or eight if you have done CAD drawings, testing, a prototype or even tooling, and say it is hard to get over 10 because Disney gets over 10 and you are not Disney [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:05:24]. The base also differs: Brian Fried says his royalty is typically a percentage of the wholesale price the licensee charges the buyer, paid quarterly with sell-through reports by store and variation [UnGdjQb467o @ 00:01:58]. A quoted percentage means nothing until you pin whether it rides on gross sales or wholesale, and how much development you already absorbed for the company.

Negotiating posture splits the camp. Sef Chang refuses to open with a number: he asks whether the company is interested, lets it contact manufacturers, pull quotes and compute its own profit, then demands the cost rundown and moves the needle back and forth until both sides are comfortable, trading for something else of value if the percentage lands low [bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:01:24]. J.D. Houvener of Bold Patents takes the opposite stance and walks in armed: a perfect-deal target plus hard walk-away terms such as at least four percent royalty or an exclusive grant, which he says gives you posture and keeps you professional and unemotional at the table [ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:02:45]. Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss land in between, warning that the rate is only one lever; if the company says three and you want four, you can recover it through higher minimum guarantees, guaranteed sales figures that return the rights if missed, or having the licensee pay for your patents [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:03:20]. Jeff Schell adds a fourth trade the others do not price: under an exclusive arrangement, settle for slightly lower royalties if it moves the expensive obligation to enforce the patent onto the licensee [cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:02:52]. Across all four, the percentage is currency to spend, not the scoreboard itself.

Exclusivity and exit route are where the playbooks fork hardest. Jeff Schell ranks the grants cleanly: an exclusive license locks out everyone including the patent holder and usually pays the highest royalties, a sole license leaves you and one licensee in the market for a middle rate, and a non-exclusive license lets multiple companies pay you at less per licensee [cfPpWt8cw64 @ 00:01:08]. Sef Chang treats exclusivity as a walk-away issue: if he knows one company does a good job on one side of the market and another owns the other side, he will refuse an exclusive and leave rather than give it up [bO09tLv7ysM @ 00:02:51]. On building versus licensing, Andrew Krauss frames it as pure arithmetic, a 20% profit margin on 5,000 to 20,000 units while working 60 to 80 hour weeks against a licensee moving half a million units a year while you do no work [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:04:09]. J.D. Houvener describes the third route, an outright sale, as freeing you from monitoring the licensee but warns the buyer may sit on or shelve the patent, so the product never ships and you may have negotiated away your own ability to iterate in that space [2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:07:18]. Choose the route by volume, by control, and by how much business you actually want to run.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Stephen Key is blunt that not every license pays. His novelty run produced Sweet Darts, a plastic suction-cup arrow that sold during one Valentine's season for about $10,000, plus back-to-school spinner pins, Cool Pals lunch-box ice packs and roughly 30 plush characters that each landed around $10,000 or less [gxeuCPaGeHY @ 00:00:36]. He says the Sweet Darts money never repeated and that seasonal deals felt too much like work, which is why he did not like that industry very much [Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:03:14]. Even his winners carried haircuts: the Michael Jordan Wall Ball was a split royalty where his partner took half [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:05:09]. Brian Walker on inventRightTV shows the other end of the curve. His light chaser, built in three hours from parts already in his shop, nearly disappeared after he licensed it to SRM Entertainment because it sat unexplained in little boxes on novelty shelves until it moved into Barnum & Bailey, Universal and Disney. He expected his $5,000 advance to be all the money he would ever see, yet it generated about $10 million in royalties, a third of which went to his agent [WEVVJ111b8o @ 00:04:33]. The economics check: price the season, the split and the agent cut before celebrating any headline royalty number, and do not write off a slow starter too early.

Time is the silent cost line. Key says royalties do not start the minute you sign: the licensee has to make it, ship it and get it on the shelf, then you wait a couple of months to collect and longer for distribution to grow, so you are talking a year, a year and a half, or two years before checks really add up [Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:06:40]. Brian Walker has seen licenses produce royalties in six or seven months but says a year or more is more common, and the drag scales with tooling: his light chaser line needed a roughly 15-cavity mold and about 30 components, while his six-part animating product can reach production far faster [WEVVJ111b8o @ 00:12:56]. Walker also burned his own protection, filing about six provisional patents and letting every one expire because he was too lazy to push them within the one-year window [WEVVJ111b8o @ 00:11:22]. Key's counter-discipline is to never pour serious money into one favorite idea, and he warns that choosing the wrong idea means years go by without income; if you honestly count up all the time spent, you are not saving money on a budget, you are losing it [hM7gpPqIDoQ @ 00:19:05]. Budget the calendar as hard as the cash.

Most self-inflicted losses happen at the table or after the ink dries. Krauss says many students arrive after toploading a deal with demands like $100,000 upfront plus a 20% royalty, asks that are just not practical and that come from not knowing what the other side is doing [5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:01:06]. J.D. Houvener warns newcomers who assume the license runs for the full twenty-year patent life; both sides want to return to the table after a commercially reasonable period, and since there are no patent police, the owner must hunt infringers and get an exclusive licensee contractually on the hook to help [ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:06:10]. In a separate briefing he flags the version-two trap, where the manufacturer develops an improved variant during tooling or fabrication and tries to claim it unless the contract settles who owns what, alongside terminating if the licensee sits on the product [2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:05:03]. Key admits he dropped the ball himself after traveling for six months and coming home to find things with his licensees not quite right, and he insists on a recap email after every conversation and never going around the person you work with [hbfKyomYp6U @ 00:05:56]. A signed license is a business you still have to run.

callout.title: Do Not Sign Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, a stall or a dead deal the practitioners lived through. Clear all four before accepting a royalty offer.
items: Run the volume math first: licensee store count times roughly one sale a week per store, charted at 3%, 4%, 5% and 6%; if the volume is not there, walk or give only a non-exclusive [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:02:17].
Lock minimum guarantees and required sales figures so the rights come back to you if the licensee does not perform [inventRightTV — 5pNsi_2H-J4 @ 00:03:37].

Write ownership of improvements and version two into the contract, plus termination if the licensee sits on the product instead of manufacturing it [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — 2yLgmvphmBw @ 00:05:03].
Budget one to two years from signature before royalties really add up, and keep your day job funding the gap [inventRightTV — Se-TzTVqhfY @ 00:06:40].

Write down your perfect-deal goals and your walk-away terms, such as a minimum royalty or exclusivity, before you sit at the table [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — ZbJhX8I0koA @ 00:02:26].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find receptive companies, present my product idea and turn outreach into a licensing deal?
chapters.title: Find Licensees and Pitch the Product
chapters.subtitle: Potential-licensee lists, open-innovation companies, company requirements, product pitches, unanswered outreach and AI-assisted commercialization
chapters.executive_summary: Stephen Key, Andrew Krauss, Gateway's outreach team and Mark Reyland converge on one model: build a fit-checked list of 20 to 30 licensees, reach them through permission-based LinkedIn, email and phone outreach rather than portals, and arrive with a filed provisional, a works-like prototype and a one-sentence benefit. The numbers are concrete: ten connections per company, five companies in 30 minutes, follow-ups every five days with success at six to seven touches, provisionals near $60 to $65, and royalties of 5 to 8 percent on wholesale, with Reyland citing an 8 percent average. Disagreements are real: Krauss says many companies still hold at 5 percent, Key skips NDAs once a provisional is filed while Reyland asks companies to sign the inventor's own, and phone has dropped from first to last even as Chad insists on picking up the phone.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this roster treats licensing as a volume game run through relationships, not a lottery ticket mailed to a portal. Stephen Key states flatly that you might need to reach 20 to 30 companies before one does a deal, and that most inventors never bother to do that [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:00:51]. The hit list should hold at least 20 companies; Key calls a list of five "not great" and builds the list by walking the Walmart aisle where the product belongs, asking the manager, photographing packaging, and harvesting 800 numbers [mljygoL-peE @ 00:01:06]. Mark Reyland runs the same shelf harvest, photographing the maker information printed on package backs, loading it into a spreadsheet, and then shopping the product through each company's own submission process [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:22:52]. The Gateway outreach team puts hard numbers on the grind: Dana reports that reaching 52 companies took 500 to 1,000 touches, and Chad says he contacted over 200 companies before licensing anything, iterating on every round of feedback [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:30:34]. Chad's warning cuts the other way too: blasting "37 emails to who?" is wasted motion unless every message lands on a decision-maker. The baseline expectation is months of disciplined outreach, not a single lucky pitch.

Practitioners agree that the cold portal is dead weight and that permission-based relationships close deals. Key reports hearing from companies that they don't really license ideas from the portal, endorses only Oxo and Hasbro Spark, and warns never to pay a portal [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:07:35]. Portals, in Key's words, are "for people that are just starting out," so even when a company runs one, the move is LinkedIn with a strong profile and a short script asking whether the company participates in open innovation, which is explicitly "asking for permission" [biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:01:48]. Permission is leverage: per the Licensing Playbook crew, it buys the right to follow up for six months, while an unsolicited send earns "maybe twice" [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:16:40]. Thirty contacts means thirty relationships, and companies usually take the third or fourth idea from an inventor they already trust. Key also stresses that the old FedEx-next-day approach is finished; email overload and automation mean "it is who you know today" [LWNWc2dynPI @ 00:15:31]. The shared filter for who deserves those relationships is fit: Key prefers companies with an outside-submission department and walks away when a mega-company demands an issued patent, because the game is speed to market rather than protection.

The third pillar of agreement is skin in the game before the pitch: a filed provisional, a works-like prototype, and a benefit you can say in one breath. Gateway's Dana Nolles says the team needs to see "that your product does what you're saying it does," and a duct-taped or glued works-like prototype is enough, while an issued patent and even a sell sheet are not required to apply [p3ODWhpvt3E @ 00:02:07]. Key files a provisional before approaching companies, $65 in the start-to-finish walkthrough, and writes it around why the idea wasn't done before, packed with variations and workarounds [LWNWc2dynPI @ 00:05:30]. Reyland lands in the same place from a different angle: under 20 percent of retail products carry any patent protection, so file a provisional right before approaching companies and go back to the drawing board if no license arrives within 12 months [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:01:46]. On messaging, Key calls the ability to describe the benefit in one sentence one of the most important things you can do today, and builds every pitch around that single USP [KOR6yXD1nTQ @ 00:05:17]. The idea itself, Key estimates, is only five to ten percent of the process.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The outreach engine starts on LinkedIn. Key's current channel order is LinkedIn first, direct email second using addresses found through Email Hunter or Apollo, and phone last, a full reversal from the days when phone led [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:08:39]. The mechanical play: connect with about ten people per company with no message attached, covering five companies in 30 minutes; one member's fast-food outreach drew roughly 90 percent responses within two hours [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:20:54]. The profile itself needs a smiling photo and a simple innovation-themed banner rather than the product, because companies check it first, and outreach should hit at least five people per company across marketing, sales and new product development, stopping once one answers [aFZpyTUvtlY @ 00:00:54]. The message runs two to three lines: IP status, what the product is, and its benefit, followed by an offer of a sell sheet or one-minute video and a request for a referral to the right person. Once interest lands, move off LinkedIn to Zoom, Skype or phone, test the audio, keep dogs and kids out of the room, and prepare for five questions on IP, prior art, prototype, pricing and costs [biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:04:35].

Follow-up cadence is where the street numbers get specific. Key cites data that 48 percent of people never follow up and 25 percent follow up only twice, while success arrives at six to seven follow-ups spaced five days apart, not "a couple weeks," and logged in a tracking chart [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:27:54]. Krauss adds a cleaner nudge: forward the original email rather than asking "did you get my email" [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:31:03]. The Licensing Playbook crew benchmarks two to three follow-ups on average and six to eight as the ceiling, after which you find another contact at the same company and reference the prior one. Dana's "triple threat" fires voicemail, LinkedIn and email inside 15 minutes, and Chad calls with the email open on screen because in 90 percent of cases the contact has already seen it [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:14:47]. When a contact goes dark, Key uses the "I" word, "I'm concerned... is everything okay," framing the note around the person rather than the product, and reports a reply "almost every single time," usually opening with "I'm so sorry" [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:04:54]. Krauss's own blunt variant, "just give me a yes or no," pulled an answer within a minute.

The collateral and cost stack is cheap by design. Key paid $800 for a first sell sheet in Modesto; now Key voice-dictates every feature into ChatGPT Pro, asks for ten USPs, and tailors them by audience and length, while Krauss prefers Claude, and paid tiers run about $20 [KOR6yXD1nTQ @ 00:25:39]. Krauss wants a sell sheet readable in six seconds, with a competitive-analysis second page and 3D renderings, never a 25-page PowerPoint [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:40:40]. A provisional runs about $60 to $65, Smart IP software $99, and the target is under a year to test interest [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:25:39]. On the back end, Key pegs royalties at 5 to 8 percent, usually on wholesale against roughly a 20 percent company margin. Reyland's numbers put the National Royalty Guide average at 8 percent, cap personal deals at 10 percent, and place most deals near 6 percent and As Seen On TV deals near 2.5 percent. The performance guarantee math uses Home Depot: 700 stores at 1.5 units a week is about 1,100 a week, with the minimum set at 60 to 70 percent of that, backed by a store manager's movement report [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:32:03].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among these operators is over the front door. Stephen Key tells operators to ignore the submit button and work LinkedIn even when a portal exists, calling portals a channel “for people that are just starting out” [biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:01:48]. Pressed on portals, Key goes further: companies have said they don't really license ideas from portals, only Oxo and Hasbro Spark earn an endorsement, and any portal that charges a fee gets a hard no [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:07:35]. Elsewhere Key flips the filter, telling operators to favor companies that already run a department for outside submissions, because a company without a process forces you to educate them and moves slowly [MvycxV2ib_8 @ 00:01:49]. Mark Reyland sits on the opposite side of the portal debate entirely: photograph the maker information on package backs, load it into a spreadsheet, and then follow each company's own submission process rather than going around it [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:22:52]. The bridge follows from Key's own script of “asking for permission”: open with a person on LinkedIn, ask whether the company participates in open innovation, and route materials through whatever intake the company already runs.

Protection posture is the second fault line. Key personally skips the NDA once a provisional is on file and warns that demanding a company sign your paper can make them “hang up” [biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:08:30]. Key and Krauss time the ask instead: request one only when the company asks for IP or a prototype, so “the clock doesn't start on your intellectual property” [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:49:09]. Mark Reyland runs the opposite play: have an attorney draft your own NDA once, because enforcement varies state by state, never download a template, and ask each company to sign yours, while accepting that a refusal does not make them crooked and that every NDA must expire [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:14:21]. The patent split runs just as deep. Key treats a mega-company demanding an issued patent as a signal to move on, since the game is “speed to market” [MvycxV2ib_8 @ 00:02:38], and Reyland backs the logic with numbers: under 20 percent of retail products carry any patent protection, and a roughly $12,000 utility patent buys a less than 50/50 shot. For the operator, that means a $60-to-$65 provisional filed as a selling tool is the shared floor, while the NDA posture is the live choice between Key's speed and Reyland's paper.

Numbers diverge once the conversation turns to money and cadence. Key pegs royalties at 5 to 8 percent with consumables slightly lower, while Krauss pushes back that many companies still hold at 5 percent [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:44:55]. Reyland quotes an 8 percent average from the National Royalty Guide, yet most Reyland deals land near 6 percent, the ceiling is 10, and As Seen On TV deals sit near 2.5 percent [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:32:03]. On the first call, though, Key and Krauss say never name a rate at all: claim flexibility and turn the question back by asking what their last licensing agreement looked like [zdIFauqdSt8 @ 00:12:49]. Channel order splits too. Key now ranks LinkedIn first, email second and phone dead last after four months of personal pitching, but Chad's counter is blunt: “Pick up the phone and call them,” because in 90 percent of cases the contact has already seen the email, and Dana stacks voicemail, LinkedIn and email inside 15 minutes [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:13:39]. Follow-up math also conflicts: Key's rule is every five days until the sixth or seventh touch, while Chad and Dana report two to three follow-ups on average and six to eight at most before switching to a new contact.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest mistakes are cash spent before a single company says yes. Key reports $10,000 to $12,000 spent on licensing agents with zero results, one request for a trade-show booth success that turned up none, and a $10,000 patent followed by another $10,000 for changes [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:51:11]. Calling the wrong companies, Key warns, burns “tens of thousands of dollars” and leaves a worthless patent as a “plaque on the wall” [MvycxV2ib_8 @ 00:00:07]. Key's closing fix in that warning is to learn the language of licensing and be patient. Gateway's Dana Nolles and Key put a hard number on the manufacture-first trap: making product earns no royalty bump unless roughly 300,000 units moved that year, so spending $100,000 to sell units first is not worth it, and buyers want new products anyway [p3ODWhpvt3E @ 00:07:02]. Even Gateway, at $6,000, only accepts clients when 99.9 percent confident and claims a 100 percent success rate or money back. The base rate is brutal on every channel. Key says most patents never make a dime, and the Patent Attorney Worldwide pitch puts the figure at about 95 percent of patents that “never ever make a single rupee” [B-E0dIbeMfg @ 00:00:13].

Inside the room, most deals die from behavior. Key and Krauss say a failed first meeting means “the deal's done,” so the move is to stop selling, listen and ask questions, because 80 percent of closable deals die when the inventor doesn't know what they are doing [zdIFauqdSt8 @ 00:16:46]. The classic overreach is raising royalty rates, minimum guarantees or deal structure after a single call; Key says companies “are going to run,” and that a licensing agreement should be requested only after they say “we're interested” [biVTpLl2T5U @ 00:12:35]. Overselling and market-share math are the next traps: capture-10-percent-of-the-market claims are a red flag, as is waving other suitors around instead of citing an NDA, and Key separately bars “billion dollar” claims and links from the opening message. Sloppy automation kills outreach before any meeting: the panel warns that copy-paste scripts can land a competitor's name in the message, and the hosts push full customization over Mailchimp-style blasts [LO-vI8icz70 @ 00:52:58]. Unsolicited sends backfire too: a CEO once got angry at a sell sheet nobody asked for, so permission still comes first [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 01:07:09].

Before signing, run the unit math the way these operators do. Reyland sets the performance guarantee from store velocity: 700 Home Depot stores at 1.5 units a week is roughly 1,100 a week, the minimum lands at 60 to 70 percent of that, and a store manager's movement report supplies the real figure [71FE9YR_9no @ 00:28:11]. Reyland also wants upfront money because shelf time can stretch to about 1.5 years, and refuses to ever assign the patent, since the licensing contract already works as a pseudo assignment. Key's retail test is the companion check: one sale a week across 20,000 stores is 20,000 units a week, and knowing the category's $10 to $20 price band tells you the licensee's profit and justifies a bigger royalty [G2JXLQrTZXI @ 00:29:45]. Royalties usually ride on wholesale against roughly a 20 percent company margin, and Key flags two structural leaks: Pepsi pays only a one-time fee, so license to its supplier, and a $10 million software deal missed a $5 million sublicense share [IMLF0c7wOQI @ 00:56:37]. Price is the final gate: Key and Krauss call it the number one reason products get kicked out [1w_iTE7ZNso @ 00:50:47].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I negotiate a licensing term sheet and agreement that addresses compensation, exclusivity, duration and control of the rights?
chapters.title: Negotiate the License and Term Sheet
chapters.subtitle: Royalties and equity, exclusive versus non-exclusive rights, binding clauses, joint development, board-game rights duration, reversion and sublicensing
chapters.executive_summary: Licensing operators converge on one playbook: lock the commercial skeleton in a short term sheet, then fight over scope, money, and exit triggers in the definitive license. Term sheets are treated as non-binding except for exclusivity/no-shop and confidentiality, with expenses and validity dates sometimes binding too. Grant of rights is negotiated as a matrix of exclusivity, field, territory, and manufacture/use/sell rights, never handing over unvalued rights. Street numbers: royalties typically land at 3 to 7 percent with 5 percent as the anchor, industry bands run 0.1 to 25 percent, university equity runs 2 to 5 percent, and one board game publisher asks for five-year terms. Disagreements surface on exclusive versus non-exclusive economics, distribution reach versus headline rate, and whether rights revert when a licensee company is sold.

key_metrics.context: Ryan Stewart's answer when pinned down on a typical product licensing royalty; final rate moves with category, leverage, and whether the product is already proven in the market.

key_metrics.context: Range of royalty rates as a percentage of sales or profits, varying widely by industry, patent strength, competition, and commercialization stage.
