sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The first consensus point is that the term sheet is a map, not a contract. Ryan Floyd of Storm Ventures calls it a non-binding agreement whose job is to summarize the principal economic and governance terms so nothing major is still unresolved when the legal agreement gets drafted, and he warns that any big issue that matters to you must be written in, because the other side will certainly write in theirs [f7jKIsIKO1c @ 00:00:35]. He counts only two binding provisions: exclusivity, meaning you stop shopping the deal to other parties once you sign, and confidentiality [f7jKIsIKO1c @ 00:01:05]. Campus Fund describes term sheets as morally binding but legally not binding, and lists four clauses that typically do bite at signing: exclusivity or no-shop, confidentiality, expenses, and a validity date after which the sheet automatically lapses unless definitive agreements are signed [rbNcenaCppU @ 00:01:37]. The docstocTV checklist adds that the expenses clause can itself be binding and obligate one party to pay the other side's expenses if the transaction does not proceed, while in other deals it stays non-binding until definitive documentation, so that single provision deserves a careful read before anything is signed [HbM8XU4hPCc @ 00:02:20]. Whatever lands in that sheet sets the frame for the definitive license, so a licensor's money terms belong there from day one.

Every practitioner who drafts licenses treats the grant of rights as the core asset being sold. John Baxter opens every agreement with the scope question: exclusive, sole, or non-exclusive, with a sole license defined as exclusive except that the licensor also keeps commercial rights to exploit the technology itself, and the deciding question being whether other licensees will be needed now or later [yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:01:11]. He then layers manufacture, use, and sell rights, territory, application field, the exact IP being licensed, and sublicensing or have-made rights into a matrix, and gives the example of hydraulic IP licensed for earth-moving equipment over 10 tons in one territory and for forklift trucks under five tons in another [yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:03:14]. His rule is to analyze that matrix cell by cell and never grant commercially unnecessary, and therefore unvalued, rights. Bao Tran runs the same play from the licensor side, partitioning field of use, such as heart treatment versus diabetic treatment, separately from territory so the patent owner can extract more value from each slice [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:10:49]. Andrew Ayers adds the enforcement angle: the single most important feature of an exclusive license is the right to sue and stop anyone else from using the licensed product [lVFYoVaNnrs @ 00:02:17].

The third point of agreement is that an exclusive grant without performance teeth is a trap. J.D. Houvener warns that going exclusive puts a lot of eggs in one basket and insists on a performance clause so that if the licensee decides to shelve the product you can get out of the contract, while noting the upside that an exclusive licensee is usually on the hook, sometimes contractually, to help enforce the rights against infringers [-VhDIVEwvzI @ 00:00:44]. UpCounsel names failing to secure performance obligations that force the licensee to hit specific milestones, and setting inadequate royalty rates, as the two common mistakes that cap an inventor's profit [Lpv4Uq-cOLA @ 00:01:19]. Bao Tran pushes further: anticipate that product development will not go as planned, write plan B into the agreement, understand what is and is not in the licensee's control, and negotiate an explicit right to terminate on a missed milestone, which he separates from a softer good-faith duty to renegotiate the milestones [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:13:01]. Baxter closes the loop on the money: never warrant the validity of your own patent, insist on the right to inspect the licensee's financial accounts and sales records, and make the audit clause cover what happens whether it reveals underpayment or overpayment [NU_eh8zb6Uk @ 00:00:46].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On rate, Ryan Stewart of Licensing Basics pins the typical royalty at about 5 percent, with 3 to 7 percent as the average band, and says the final figure moves with the product category, your leverage, and whether the product is already selling or is still a napkin drawing that forces the company to put far more at risk in development and manufacturing [uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:02:31]. His headline lesson, though, is that distribution beats rate: a 12 percent royalty from a company sitting in roughly 50 stores produces a small check, while 3 percent from a company in every big-box outlet and thousands of stores can pay far more [uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:01:00]. UpCounsel's benchmark sheet puts software at 8 to 12 percent, pharmaceuticals and biotech at 6 to 10, electronics at 4.8 to 5.5, aerospace at 3.5 to 4.5, and automotive at 3 to 3.8 [cURFfKlt_Ek @ 00:00:34]. The same source anchors valuation on the rule of 25 percent of pre-tax operating profit from the licensed product, alongside profit split, residual income, and risk-adjusted models, and tells negotiators to pull comparable deals from KT Mine and Royalty Source while weighing the licensee's margins, since higher margins can justify a higher rate [cURFfKlt_Ek @ 00:01:16].

Structure matters as much as rate. Baxter's baseline remuneration package is an upfront license or disclosure fee plus either a once-only royalty, which can be stage-gated, or a per-unit royalty expressed as a percentage of sale price or a fixed currency amount per unit, sometimes topped with an annual minimum royalty [yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:04:02]. Bao Tran splits the money by stage: expense reimbursement of patent costs, development milestone payments per country or per licensed product, and maintenance fees before sales, then annual minimum royalties, running royalties, sublicense fees, tiers that may step down over time, and sales milestones once product ships [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:07:31]. On equity he repeats the VC line that nine out of ten companies fail, so a stake carries roughly 90 percent odds of being worth nothing, which is why universities typically take 2 to 5 percent as a substitute for upfront cash that startups lack, never as a substitute for royalties, giving the licensor another leg for the exit [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:09:28]. Trenner, who negotiated licenses from the inside as senior patent counsel at a national lab, reduces it to the question inventors fumble: upfront payments, royalties per unit, or performance milestones, and how the deal shares risk [dSzZD5CnwK8 @ 00:03:52].

Clock terms are where the board game trade gives the hardest numbers. The Flatlined Games operator behind Boardgame Publisher has seen three to four years pass between first agreement and a finished game, and sets the publish-by window at two to three years, because promising next year voids the contract if it slips, while promising ten years gets refused by any designer who doubts the company will still exist [SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:01:42]. Once published he wants five years of publication rights, followed by automatic renewal one year at a time for as long as the game keeps reprinting and selling, with the designer able to reclaim rights and have the publisher sell out remaining stock if volumes disappoint [SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:02:30]. His sublicensing model is a reserved right written into the designer contract from day one: he publishes French, English, Dutch, and German editions himself and sublicenses the rest by language or territory, such as all of North America to Stronghold Games for Steamrollers and Polish-language rights to Portal Games [SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:08:06]. Getting the final paper checked is cheap by comparison: ContractsCounsel puts the average flat-fee review at $440 across dozens of projects, rising with location, contract length, complexity, and whether redlining and negotiation are added [U51x7R7u71M @ 00:03:45].

callout.title: Small clauses that move real money
callout.body: Four drafting moves practitioners use to protect the royalty stream and keep pending-stage deals alive.
items: Foreign-currency royalties can deliver an exchange gain or lose badly; if you are driven to a fixed royalty in a foreign currency, always provide for proper indexation [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:04:55]

You do not need to wait for grant to license: when licensing a pending patent, include a clause specifying that rights become active upon patent grant, and file before disclosing details [UpCounsel — AaEw4SGbkk0 @ 00:02:27]
Know-how being licensed should be properly documented, and at the very least listed in summary bullet form, so it can actually be defined in the grant [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:02:40]

Use a hybrid model of upfront fees plus ongoing royalties to balance risk and reward, and add rate-adjustment provisions tied to sales performance or industry shifts [UpCounsel — cURFfKlt_Ek @ 00:01:35]

sop_steps.title: Lock the term sheet skeleton
sop_steps.action: Draft a short term sheet naming parties, consideration, and the binding clauses before any definitive license work.
sop_steps.detail: Treat exclusivity/no-shop, confidentiality, expenses, and validity expiry as the clauses that bind [Campus Fund — rbNcenaCppU @ 00:01:03], and spell out who gets paid, how much, when, in what form, and who is obligated to pay [docstocTV — HbM8XU4hPCc @ 00:01:20].

sop_steps.title: Build the grant-of-rights matrix
sop_steps.action: Map exclusivity, manufacture/use/sell, territory, field, licensed IP, and sublicensing as separate cells.
sop_steps.detail: Analyze the rights using a rigid matrix cell by cell and never grant commercially unnecessary, unvalued rights to a licensee [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:03:46].

sop_steps.title: Price against distribution and leverage
sop_steps.action: Set the royalty after sizing the licensee's store count and how central the IP is to the product.
sop_steps.detail: A 3 percent rate across thousands of big-box stores can beat 12 percent in 50 stores [Licensing Basics — uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:01:20]; if the IP covers core product value the licensee negotiates from the weaker position, if only a minor fraction it pushes hard to cut cost [Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney — SkIAUEkenak @ 00:06:10].

sop_steps.title: Wire performance, audit, and reversion triggers
sop_steps.action: Add milestone termination, audit rights, and automatic reversion events before signing.
sop_steps.detail: Negotiate an explicit right to terminate on missed milestones [Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney — SkIAUEkenak @ 00:13:01], audit accounts covering under- and overpayment [BaxterIPAttorneys — NU_eh8zb6Uk @ 00:00:46], and automatic reversion if the licensee goes bankrupt or ceases to exist [Boardgame Publisher — SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:04:37].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Ryan Stewart of Licensing Basics ranks distribution above the royalty rate: a twelve percent royalty from a company stocked in only 50 stores produces a small check, while a 3% royalty from a licensee in every big-box store and thousands of outlets can pay far more [uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:01:00]. When pinned down, Stewart puts the typical royalty at about 5%, with 3 to 7 percent as the average band [uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:02:31]. UpCounsel works from a much wider, formula-driven map: rates running from 0.1% to 25%, software at 8 to 12%, pharmaceuticals and biotech at 6 to 10%, aerospace at 3.5 to 4.5%, and automotive at 3 to 3.8%, plus the rule of 25% that hands the inventor a quarter of the pre-tax operating profit from the licensed product [cURFfKlt_Ek @ 00:00:52]. Bao Tran adds the licensee's counter-play: a company taking the long view pushes for fixed-fee and fully paid agreements so that higher sales never raise its cost [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:08:26]. The result is a split playbook. Stewart's camp negotiates the size of the shelf footprint first and treats percentage points as secondary, while UpCounsel's camp anchors the number on industry benchmarks, comparable deals pulled from KT Mine and Royalty Source, and the licensee's profit margins.

Exclusivity splits the room. Andrew Ayers tells clients who are intent on protecting a product to use the exclusive license, because its most important feature is the ability to sue and stop anyone else using the licensed product, yet concedes a non-exclusive license could make a lot more money because more people can use it [lVFYoVaNnrs @ 00:03:25]. J.D. Houvener frames exclusivity as putting a lot of eggs in one basket that has to be managed harder, pushing for a performance clause so the licensor can exit if the licensee shelves the product, while flagging the upside that an exclusive licensee is usually on the hook for infringement protection because it is fully vested [-VhDIVEwvzI @ 00:00:44]. UpCounsel's own videos do not describe the transfer the same way: one says an exclusive license transfers all ownership rights to the licensee while the licensor keeps title [Lpv4Uq-cOLA @ 00:00:32], the other says it transfers certain ownership rights, including the right to sue for infringement, and can be fenced by field or territory [AaEw4SGbkk0 @ 00:01:50]. The practical fork: Ayers warns the non-exclusive route lets a competitor down the street sign the same deal, while Houvener's non-exclusive model keeps royalties flowing from multiple manufacturers and retailers at once.

On the term sheet itself, the practitioners disagree on how much actually binds. Ryan Floyd of Storm Ventures counts only two binding provisions, exclusivity and confidentiality, and calls everything else an understanding about terms rather than an agreement [f7jKIsIKO1c @ 00:01:22]. Campus Fund lists four binding clauses, adding expenses and a validity date after which the term sheet automatically lapses unless definitive agreements are signed, and describes the remainder as morally binding but legally not binding [rbNcenaCppU @ 00:01:37]. docstocTV splits the difference: the expenses provision may be binding and force one party to pay the other's costs if the deal dies, or may stay non-binding until definitive documentation, and exclusivity is not always included at all [HbM8XU4hPCc @ 00:02:20]. The camps also diverge on effort. Campus Fund says not to overindex on the term sheet or let it slow the transaction, while Floyd warns that whatever terms go in are likely to persist throughout the existence of the business, so big economic and governance issues must be settled there first. On payment form, Bao Tran sets equity apart from royalty: universities take 2 to 5% of a startup's equity in place of upfront cash, knowing nine out of 10 companies fail [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:09:28].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The Boardgame Publisher operator behind Flatlined Games has lived the timeline trap: some titles took more than three or four years from first agreement with the designer to a published game [SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:00:51]. Write 'published next year' and miss it, and the contract is null and void, forcing a renegotiation from a bad position; write ten years and the designer will not agree, because the company may not exist by then. The working ballpark is two to three years to publication, then five years of publication rights with an automatic one-year renewal while reprints continue. The economics check is blunt: if a 3,000-copy print run would take ten years to sell through, reprinting makes no sense, the contract lapses, and the rights revert to the designer [SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:04:07]. Bao Tran tells licensors to assume product development will not go as planned, write plan B into the agreement, and negotiate an explicit right to terminate on a missed milestone, which differs from a good-faith promise to renegotiate milestones [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:13:01]. UpCounsel names the same failure from the inventor side: not securing performance obligations that force the licensee to hit specific milestones, alongside setting inadequate royalty rates that cap the inventor's profits [Lpv4Uq-cOLA @ 00:01:19].

John Baxter of Baxter IP flags currency as the quiet loss: a royalty set in a foreign currency can win on exchange gains, but a licensor can also lose and lose badly if driven to a fixed royalty in a foreign currency, so always provide proper indexation [yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:05:12]. Per-unit dollar royalties should likewise be indexed for inflation, and remuneration wording must be unambiguous enough to survive interpretation by a court. In a follow-up session Baxter adds two traps: never warrant the validity of the licensor's patent, and write audit provisions that cover the awkward case where the audit turns up either underpayment or overpayment of royalty [NU_eh8zb6Uk @ 00:01:02]. Ryan Floyd shows how headline numbers mislead in a term sheet: at $8 million pre-money with a $2 million raise and a 10% post-money option pool, the effective pre-money drops to $7 million, and converting notes and warrants collapse into that same calculation [f7jKIsIKO1c @ 00:03:18]. Floyd's rule is that the option pool is really just a valuation discussion: a bigger pool means a lower effective pre-money. Trenner Law Firm, which negotiated licensing deals from inside a national lab, says many inventors lose out at exactly this stage because they do not understand the mechanics of the deal [dSzZD5CnwK8 @ 00:04:12].

The surprise Andrew Ayers warns clients about is believing they signed an exclusive license and later finding it was non-exclusive, with no ability to stop the competitor down the street from adopting the same software [lVFYoVaNnrs @ 00:04:49]. Trenner Law Firm warns against targeting the wrong licensees: if an invention requires a company to build an entirely new factory, it probably will not license it, and approaching the wrong targets wastes everyone's time and can prematurely wear out interest in the invention [dSzZD5CnwK8 @ 00:02:53]. UpCounsel's mistake list runs from insufficient research on licensees and weak or vague agreements to sharing technical details without protection and overvaluing the patent, and it warns that royalty income can be inconsistent and licensee compliance must be monitored [AaEw4SGbkk0 @ 00:05:23]. Bao Tran describes the counterparty's hardball play, which Tran calls ethically questionable: the efficient infringement approach, where a company practices the claimed invention and forces the owner to prove validity and infringement, front-loading the owner's expenses while carrying significant risk for the company if infringement is found [SkIAUEkenak @ 00:04:38]. That is the leverage reality: a patent covering the core of a product puts the licensee in the weaker seat, while one touching a minor fraction lets the licensee negotiate the price down hard.

callout.title: Kill-Switch Clauses to Lock Before Signature
callout.body: Every item below comes from a trap the practitioners hit or watched counterparties exploit. If any one is missing from the draft, the deal is not ready to sign.
items: Confirm in the grant language whether the license is exclusive, sole, or non-exclusive, because finding out later that it was non-exclusive leaves no way to stop a competitor [Ayers Law TV ~ Andrew M. Ayers, Esq. — lVFYoVaNnrs @ 00:04:35].
Attach a performance clause to any exclusive grant so the licensor can exit if the licensee shelves the product [J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm — -VhDIVEwvzI @ 00:00:58].
Index every per-unit or foreign currency royalty, since a fixed royalty in a foreign currency can lose badly [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:05:12].
Write automatic reversion triggers for bankruptcy, the licensee ceasing to operate, and out-of-print status before the deal closes [Boardgame Publisher — SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:04:37].

chapters.pull_quote: "When it comes down to a licensing agreement, distribution is much more important than the specific royalty rate." Ryan Stewart, Licensing Basics (uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:01:40).
action_checklist: Map the grant as a matrix of exclusivity, manufacture/use/sell rights, territory, field, licensed IP, and sublicensing, and never grant commercially unnecessary rights for free [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:03:14].
Ask how many stores the licensee distributes into before haggling the rate, then negotiate inside the 3 to 7 percent band around a typical 5% [Licensing Basics — uBnJLlSWMLk @ 00:02:31].
Negotiate an explicit right to terminate on a missed milestone rather than a good-faith promise to renegotiate milestones [Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney — SkIAUEkenak @ 00:13:01].
Express per-unit royalties as a percentage of sale price or a fixed amount indexed for inflation, and add an annual minimum royalty where possible [BaxterIPAttorneys — yl8L7tuwNuI @ 00:04:38].
Read the binding term sheet clauses on exclusivity, confidentiality, expenses, and the validity expiry date before signing anything else [Campus Fund — rbNcenaCppU @ 00:01:37].
Write rights reversion for bankruptcy, company sale, and out-of-print status into the contract from the start [Boardgame Publisher — SOV77fL52Dw @ 00:04:37].

chapters.question_prompt: How do researchers, technology-transfer offices and startups move university inventions toward commercial licensing?
chapters.title: Commercialize Research Through Technology Transfer
chapters.subtitle: MIT, Columbia, Purdue and other university commercialization offices; research patenting, startup-license financials, medical technologies and shelved patents
chapters.executive_summary: Tech transfer operators from MIT, Columbia, Ohio State, Salk, NYU, UW and FedTech agree the business is a lottery of home runs. Nelsen says only a dozen US offices make money at any time. Columbia's Herschwitz reports that 84% of universities lose money on a gross basis. Salk's director says two or three inventions drive 80-90% of revenue. The mechanics are tight. A provisional goes in before publication at $1,200-$1,500 and non-provisionals cost $15-30K. Income takes a 15% admin fee, then inventors split one-third. Startups get an option, then a license, with equity taken as deferred compensation. Royalties are back-loaded, and missing a diligence milestone triggers termination. Disagreements center on patent-first filing versus getting industry feedback before filing, and on exclusive versus non-exclusive grants: three of Columbia's four biggest earners were non-exclusive. Practitioners also split on whether foundation money is a red flag and whether a royalty ever goes up after signing.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every office head on record treats university licensing as a home-run business, not a steady earner. Lita Nelsen brokered hundreds and hundreds of MIT deals over 30-plus years. Nelsen warns that TLOs do not make money on the average. Only a dozen of the hundreds of US offices are profitable at any given time, and not always the same ones, so from a business point of view it is more like a lottery [Dd9V4RSqNuk @ 00:03:34]. Lesley Millar-Nicholson backs that with AUTM numbers from 1991 to 2022. Every $1 of research funding earned roughly 4 cents, licensing income runs 3.5 to 4% of research spend, and only 14% of US offices cover their operating costs [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:29:32]. The Salk director says offices pull 80 or 90% of revenue from two or three inventions. All the other inventions put together make up 10 to 20%, which the director calls a game of home runs [3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:07:18]. Ohio State's office measured the tail directly. Only 0.1% of all inventions ever disclosed reached $1M cumulative, against 0.8% at Stanford. Every office clearing $100M has a drug behind it, and without that drug over 90% of revenue disappears [HKAvhkDKxNQ @ 00:27:16]. The office calls it an accidental success it is hoping for, while insisting the process itself stays disciplined.

The second point of agreement is that university inventions arrive brutally early and pay slowly. Nelsen describes technology that worked in the lab and maybe in a mouse but is going to take years. Federal funding stops right around publication, while pharma only wants clinic-ready assets. Development costs tens of millions for devices and hundreds of millions for drugs [Dd9V4RSqNuk @ 00:02:47]. Millar-Nicholson maps the valley of death in three stages: 2 to 3 years to an issued patent, 2 to 3 more to form a business, and the same again to raise money. Founders are told that if they are in this for quick money, it ain't happening [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:31:16]. The MIT licensing curve is unforgiving. About 40% of patents get licensed. Of those, 89% are licensed within 5 years, 8% in years 5 to 10, and 2% after that. Once the window passes without a deal, the likelihood of licensing diminishes to near zero [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:32:38]. Herschwitz sees the same shape at Columbia. Half of eventual deals close by about year 3, and 20% are still unsigned at years 6 to 7. The curve holds regardless of field, exclusivity or royalty type, and it matches NCI, the UC system and Cornell [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:18:16].

The prerequisites are consistent across offices. First, disclose before you publish. Tiana Stewart of NYU tells PIs you can never start too early with the tech transfer office, but it can be too late. A conference counts as public disclosure, and Carolyn Jgo adds that a rushed internal disclosure gives no public protection [jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:08:52]. Second, understand what a patent actually buys. Eli Lilly patent counsel Cedric D'Hue warns that a patent is a right of exclusion, not a right to sell, and that FDA clearance is a separate gate entirely [hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:31:46]. Columbia's Herschwitz goes further: a patent does not allow you to do anything at all. It only stops someone else from doing something, which makes it a negative right [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:35:26]. Third, know the ownership chain. Millar-Nicholson lists the Bayh-Dole duties that have applied since 1980: protect, commercialize, report, prefer small business, require US manufacture, and share revenue with inventors. Those duties sit on top of MIT's roughly $800M a year in research, about 65% of it federal [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:09:51]. D'Hue adds that employees must assign IP to the university and joint work produces co-assignees. A courtesy introduction carries no IP claim, so ownership questions get settled before the money shows up.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Offices run a tight intake before any money gets spent. MIT's Lauren Foster and Deirdre Zammit triage every disclosure on three questions: problem-solution fit, disruptive versus incremental, and whether the target market has an appetite for outside innovation. Disclosures that pass are then tested for utility, novelty and non-obviousness [2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:20:05]. All patent drafting goes to external law firms, and prosecution can take three to four years. MIT files on about half of its disclosures; in FY2021 that meant 730 disclosures and about 358 US filings [2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:30:50]. The cost ladder is concrete. NYU's Tiana Stewart prices a provisional at $1,200 to $1,500. A non-provisional runs $15K to $30K, with lawyers billing $380 to $500 an hour and issuance taking 3 to 5 years. Stewart treats the provisional as a timestamp that buys one year and can be refiled if more data is needed [jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:48:53]. Columbia's Herschwitz files provisionals on about 67% of inventions and converts roughly two-thirds of them at 12 months. Costs then climb to $20K to $30K per patent by year 3, add $100K to $150K for every foreign country, and reach around $500K by years 7 to 8 [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:19:10]. That spend is why offices treat patent-cost reimbursement as non-negotiable when a startup licensee signs.

Deal structure follows a standard sequence. At MIT, an option agreement comes first, and exercising it requires a business plan. Consideration then stacks several pieces: a license fee, equity for startups only as deferred compensation, maintenance fees, a sublicensing share, milestone payments such as FDA approval, royalties and patent-cost reimbursement [2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:59:59]. Incoming money takes a 15% admin fee first and then recovers patent costs. Inventors as a pool then take one-third, while departments, labs, centers and the General Fund take two-thirds [2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:10:33]. Before any of that, faculty founder Bulović describes how MIT pays patent costs up front and asks founders for a couple grand of skin in the game. Founders get about nine months to pitch VCs and reimburse prosecution costs once funded [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:04:29]. On the startup side, the Osage panel of Lisa Norton, Rick Friedman and Nakisha Holder says terms are back-loaded as risk sharing and trade against each other, so more upfront cash or equity can mean a lower royalty. Their worked anti-dilution example is 4%, or 400,000 shares, protected through a $2M raise, which investors accept if it is cleared at the first priced round. Past patent costs above $100K get scheduled across two years, with acceleration on financing [Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 00:48:58].

Pricing and marketing are where operators earn their keep. Columbia runs 35 PhD fellows on about 100 marketing campaigns a year. Herschwitz prices from benchmark databases, moves to a term sheet, and only then brings in attorneys. The 18-page boilerplate allows royalties that step down from 5% to 1%, plus caps, minimums and buyouts, such as a clause ending the royalty for $15 million [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:58:27]. Stewart at NYU cold-emails and cold-calls companies, and listens to earnings calls to catch them early [jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:35:05]. On the open market, the USPTO licensing panel with Matt Nuccia of Design Edge and Raquel Graham quotes a 5% standard toy royalty with an advance of about 20% of first-year projected orders. The panel warns that a 1% contract can out-yield a 10% one when definitions are loose, so it insists on a sample contract first. That contract settles distribution, territory, fields of use and termination before legal fees start [AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:15:38]. Kent Richardson anchors secondary-market patent sales at about $122K per asset. A $1.2M price needs really good reasons, and $12M is six sigma territory. Richardson applies a 35% discount rule of thumb off asking prices and calls a bid and ask within 3x probably a closable deal [YwEyzgLoOrA @ 00:08:08].

callout.title: Moves the Veterans Use to Tilt University Deals
callout.body: Tactics practitioners use to strengthen claims, protect founder economics, and get in front of the right buyer before the licensing window closes.
items: Run the compound selection yourself. Whoever picks the compounds is the inventor, so outsourcing that choice hands inventorship to the other party. Push past a weak assay patent to a method-of-treatment or composition-of-matter claim [Salk Institute — 3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:40:21]

Ask that the university's liquidity fee be offset by its equity payout. On sublicenses, keep the spread between your sublicense royalty and the university royalty [Osage University Partners — Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 00:48:14]

Note which companies sponsor your conferences, because PIs' talks can get ideas stolen and industry scouts mine those talks. Flip the play by listening to earnings calls to catch companies early [American Physiological Society — jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:16:26]

Work LinkedIn and trade shows without being creepy, and ask for the inventor-relations contact. Find a person inside the company so your portal submission does not get lost; twenty no's is normal [USPTOvideo — AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:24:26]

sop_steps.title: Disclose and Timestamp
sop_steps.action: File the invention disclosure while drafting the manuscript and lock a provisional before any talk.
sop_steps.detail: Contact the office while the manuscript is in draft and expect 6 to 8 more months of data. A conference counts as public disclosure, and a provisional at $1,200 to $1,500 buys one year [American Physiological Society — jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:53:04]

sop_steps.title: Triage the Market Fit
sop_steps.action: Score problem-solution fit and confirm who pays and at what price point before converting.
sop_steps.detail: MIT triages on fit, disruptive versus incremental, and market appetite [Technology Licensing Office (TLO) — 2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:20:05]. Collins warns against a $10 solution to a 2 cent problem [USPTOvideo — hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:18:29]

sop_steps.title: Option, Then License
sop_steps.action: Sign an option first and exercise it with a business plan to secure the license.
sop_steps.detail: An option agreement precedes the license, and exercising it requires a business plan. Exclusivity can be cut by field, time or geography, while rights are retained for research, teaching, the US government and sponsors [Technology Licensing Office (TLO) — 2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:53:14]

sop_steps.title: Stack the Financials and Hit Milestones
sop_steps.action: Trade upfront cash, equity and royalty against each other, then track every diligence milestone.
sop_steps.detail: Terms are back-loaded as risk sharing. If a milestone is missed, it is considered a breach and the university can terminate the license [Osage University Partners — Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 01:22:07]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to file first or sell first. On Commercialisation Talks, the host pushes a 'reverse engineering' sequence: get industry feedback on commercial potential before committing to a filing. Telmo Santos, head of tech transfer at CCG in Portugal, says both routes should coexist. Santos concedes the real-world order is usually patentable, file, then market, because researchers want to publish, and the CCG team rarely has the people to knock on a couple of industry doors per disclosure [2_OclNjs2Hg @ 00:29:56]. The OSU tech transfer lead calls the whole model 'fundamentally a reactive business' that 'needs to be flipped around' [HKAvhkDKxNQ @ 00:16:30]. Columbia Technology Ventures' executive director comes at it from the cost line. After showing patent spend climbing to roughly $500K per patent by years seven to eight once foreign countries stack up, the director says it is 'not always the right decision to file broadly' or to file as many patents as you can [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:31:21]. NYU licensing manager Tiana Stewart pulls the opposite way on intake, telling PIs 'you can never send me enough invention disclosures' and that contact is never too early but can be too late [jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:08:52]. The working synthesis is to flood the intake, then prune hard on market evidence before the expensive non-provisional and foreign spend.

Exclusivity is the second fault line. MIT's TLO steers exclusive commercial licenses toward new ventures: 62% of its exclusive deals over the past ten years went to startup companies, while non-exclusive grants mostly go to established firms and equity is taken only from startups [2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:41:49]. Columbia's data cuts against the instinct that exclusivity equals money. Three of its four biggest earners were non-exclusive, and field-of-use exclusives sit as the middle option [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:28:03]. Lesley Millar-Nicholson's HDTV case shows how long the non-exclusive route can run even when it wins. Lim's technology was disclosed in 1989 and the standard was set in 1996, followed by roughly 13 years of little revenue. The first patent expired in 2009, infringement settlements followed, and income only hit zero around 2020, 31 years after disclosure [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:35:42]. On the startup side, the Osage panel walks through a UW coating covering boat hulls, devices and consumer products that was licensed to multiple startups instead of a single exclusive holder [Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 00:17:55]. The playbook choice is to go exclusive with equity for a venture that needs a moat to raise money. When the asset is a platform or a standard that many players must use, go non-exclusive or slice it by field.

Royalty architecture splits practitioners on both direction and definition. Columbia's executive director describes an 18-page boilerplate in which royalties can step down, for example from 5% to 1%, or step up, with caps, minimums and buyouts. The director cites a clause where 'at any point for 15 million dollars we can end the royalty rate' [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:56:14]. The Osage panel treats terms as back-loaded risk sharing, where more upfront cash or equity can buy a lower royalty [Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 00:27:36]. On escalators, one panelist says flatly, 'i don't know that i've ever seen a royalty go up' [Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 01:08:10]. The USPTO licensing panel argues the percentage itself is the wrong fight: 'I can write you a contract that gives you 1% and you can yield more than another contract that gives you 10% because the definitions aren't clear.' Their fix is an industry-specialist attorney, or a licensing agent working in that vertical [AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:17:02]. In the toy vertical, the same panel puts the standard royalty at 5%, with an advance of about 20% of first-year projected orders, and notes that medical licensing can command higher rates. The operator takeaway is to lock down the royalty base and definitions before arguing the rate, and to expect any escalator to be renegotiated rather than collected.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first economics check is that the house usually loses. Columbia's executive director reports that 84% of universities lose money on a gross basis and calls tech transfer 'a pretty bad business frankly for most universities' [ZzczaFujs3A @ 00:13:48]. MIT's Lesley Millar-Nicholson reports that only 14% of US tech transfer offices cover their operating costs, with licensing income running at just 3.5 to 4% of research funding [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:29:32]. OSU's tech transfer lead runs the breakeven math out loud. A $10M office keeping a 25% share needs $40M in revenue, which at a 2% royalty means $2B in licensee sales, and every office earning over $100M has a drug behind it [HKAvhkDKxNQ @ 00:31:16]. Salk's technology development director describes the same concentration from the inside: 80 or 90% of revenue comes from two or three inventions, and everything else together makes up 10 to 20%, 'so it really is a game of home runs' [3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:07:18]. The trap for an operator is budgeting a portfolio as if the average deal pays. Most do not. Only 40% of Columbia's licenses earn any revenue at all, so the cost base has to be underwritten by the rare outlier, not by the steady pipeline of signed deals.

The cheapest failures to prevent are disclosure and inventorship mistakes, and practitioners report these as the ones that kill assets outright. Salk's director warns that 'in every other country in the world the day that your invention is published it's no longer patentable.' The director adds that oral presentations are treated as publications outside the US [3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:47:13]. NYU's Tiana Stewart names the biggest pitfall as failing to settle inventor contribution percentages early. Stewart also notes that running experiments under someone else's direction does not make a person an inventor [jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:21:12]. Salk's director flags a subtler bench trap: whoever picks the compounds is the inventor, so outsourcing the selection hands inventorship to the outside party [3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:40:21]. Eli Lilly patent counsel Cedric D'Hue tells a war story of two PIs at different institutions collaborating with no inter-institutional agreement in place. D'Hue's prescription is NDAs, MOUs and MTAs signed up front, before any data moves [hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:46:04]. Stewart's panel reinforces the timing point by treating a conference talk as a public disclosure. Across all four accounts, the pattern is the same: the asset dies at the podium or in the lab notebook, long before any licensing conversation starts.

Execution failures hit after the deal is signed, or keep the deal from ever happening. Millar-Nicholson's curve shows that once a disclosure sits unlicensed, 'the likelihood of Licensing diminishes substantially down to near zero.' Of licensed technologies, 89% were licensed within five years, 8% in years five to ten, and 2% after ten [BtnDins-U4g @ 00:32:38]. The Osage panel warns that a missed diligence milestone 'is considered a breach of the agreement and the university will have the ability to terminate the license' [Q3YzwCiT2M4 @ 01:22:07]. The USPTO tech transfer panel reports that NC A&T's hypoallergenic peanut licensee simply lost funding, against a pharma development path that can take 'a billion dollars maybe' [hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:49:05]. On the secondary market, Kent Richardson describes a CEO who wanted $32M for a portfolio and came back asking $350,000 after reading the market report. Richardson puts a typical asset at around $122K, with asking prices discounted about 35% on average [YwEyzgLoOrA @ 00:09:14]. The economics check has three parts. Price against the median, not the dream. Put a five-year clock on every unlicensed asset. Size milestones to what a thinly funded startup licensee can actually hit, since missing them hands the university a termination right.

callout.title: Four Kill Switches to Clear Before Any Deal Moves
callout.body: Each gate below maps to an asset or deal that practitioners watched die from a preventable mistake. Clear all four before a talk, a collaboration, a grant signature, or a license draft.
items: No talk, poster, or manuscript goes public before a provisional is on file: outside the US the invention is unpatentable the day it is published, and oral presentations count as publications [Salk Institute — 3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:49:36].

Settle inventor contribution percentages early and sign NDAs, MOUs and MTAs before any cross-institution work starts, so the two-PI collaboration with no inter-institutional agreement never repeats [USPTOvideo — hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:46:04].

Read the fine print on every funder: foundation money such as Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation funding can block commercialization and is a red flag [American Physiological Society — jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:27:39].

Define the royalty base to capture the trademark and brand extensions, not just the patented product, because the trademark can be worth a thousandfold over the patent [USPTOvideo — AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:33:37].

chapters.pull_quote: "You tend to get 80 or 90% of your revenue from two or three inventions and all the other inventions put together make up 10 to 20% of your Revenue so it really is a game of home runs." — Salk Institute (3iEjObMZnZo @ 00:07:18).
action_checklist: File a provisional before any publication or conference talk; it costs about $1,200 to $1,500 and buys one year, versus $15K to $30K for a non-provisional [American Physiological Society — jxdKIK4n-Dk @ 00:48:53].
Run customer discovery before spending on patents: work out who pays and the price point, and check you are not building a $10 solution to a 2 cent problem [USPTOvideo — hwcNfSr-ia0 @ 00:18:29].

Stand up a fast-feedback bench of industry mentors, recently retired executives, MBA students, and alumni to pressure-test each disclosure's commercial potential [Commercialisation Talks — 2_OclNjs2Hg @ 00:34:09].
Start a startup with an option agreement and convert it to a full license only once a business plan is in hand to exercise it [Technology Licensing Office (TLO) — 2ADE7tP4bYM @ 00:53:14].

Get a sample contract first and settle distribution, rights territory, other fields of use, royalty definitions, and termination before lawyers draft, to cut legal fees [USPTOvideo — AcpNKjCol4s @ 00:29:05].

When selling bare patents, talk to at least three brokers, anchor on the median asset price, and treat a bid and ask within 3x as a closable deal [Schwegman Lundberg & Woessner, P.A. — YwEyzgLoOrA @ 00:15:26].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I use brand and trademark licensing to enter product categories while understanding the financial and legal commitments?
chapters.title: Build a Brand Licensing Program
chapters.subtitle: Brand versus product licensing, royalty rates, minimum guarantees, legal terms, licensing events, Disney, The Oodie and fashion-brand extensions
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree brand licensing is leasing protected IP: the licensee builds, ships and carries the risk while the licensor collects a royalty on wholesale or gross sales. Street numbers cluster: royalties run 2% to 15%, with 8% to 12% typical, hot entertainment and sports properties at 12% to 16%, food at 3% to 6%, and trading cards near 20%. The minimum guarantee is set at half the licensee's own year-one royalty projection and paid in four quarterly installments, the first on signing. Davie Fogarty's Oodie turned a first Warner Brothers drop into over $500,000 in weeks, but Fogarty warns that big-studio guarantees can sink small brands, pushing them toward niche licensors with low or zero guarantees. Operators split on control: licensors want discretionary approvals and room to exit exclusivity, licensees want fixed review windows and locked categories.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here, including the Informa licensing show team, starts from the same definition: licensing is leasing a legally protected name, character, logo or design to someone who puts it on goods and pays a royalty [TwdLXgIhXJA @ 00:00:00]. Daymond John splits it into inbound and outbound. Inbound means you lease someone else's IP, slap it on your product and pay the owner a vig; outbound means you own the asset and collect, ideally with an advance plus a percentage [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:00:51]. Stephen Key, who built Hot Picks guitar picks, found that brand licensing is product licensing run in reverse: the terms are the same, except the manufacturer is now licensing in the brand instead of an inventor licensing out an idea [WMcwXYcUD5c @ 00:02:33]. Stu Seltzer, who worked the Batman brand in-house at Warner Brothers, frames the two seats plainly. The licensor is the brand owner pushing out brand equity; the licensee is the manufacturer pulling it in to spike sales, exactly as LEGO did when it took its first-ever license, Star Wars, in 1998 while sitting near bankruptcy, and ended up with roughly half its line licensed [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:02:46]. The consensus: whichever seat you take, the money comes from borrowed consumer trust.

The second point of agreement is brutal: nobody pays for a name with no pull. Daymond John's test is whether your brand lets a licensee raise the price or move more units; if a jeans maker selling 1,000 pairs a month at $100 adds your 15% license and still moves 1,000 pairs, they are just paying you for nothing, so the license has to push them toward 10,000 pairs at $115 [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:08:15]. Seltzer screens readiness with three questions: how many people know the brand, whether they know what it stands for, and whether consumers give it permission to extend, the way Oreo can stretch into ice cream, pudding and candy; the brand also has to appeal to the end consumer, the retail buyer and the potential licensee at once [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:20:16]. Disney qualified Stephen Key on two facts before granting the guitar-pick category: a couple of years in business and placement in roughly a couple thousand stores [WMcwXYcUD5c @ 00:03:29]. The fashion-licensing channel adds the legal floor that recurs across speakers: you can only license what you own and can protect, because ownership is leverage [tHEEzY7Mwgc @ 00:01:58]. Register the trademark, prove sell-through at retail, then pitch.

Operators also agree on who carries the load. Daymond John is blunt that the licensee's responsibility is everything: make the soap, ship the soap, pay the employees, take back the returns [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:04:05]. LIMA president Mora Regan calls this the smart part of the model: a brand owner like Scotts, whose core business is soil, can license into gardening tools rather than investing out of the gate, handing the category to companies that do it better and already have distribution [KpR6WOaw0vM @ 00:01:03]. Trademark lawyer and licensing agent Marcela Dominguez makes the same pitch with Coca-Cola, which only knows beverages but can collect royalties from backpacks, bedding and toys, letting someone else put tentacles out in new categories while concentrating its own time and money on marketing, marketing, marketing [ASLTB9jyYII @ 00:02:10]. The licensee side gets its payoff too. Seltzer argues a license can deliver a sustainable competitive advantage: Breyers makes Reese's ice cream and no competitor can, and a tool seller carrying the Scotts name holds a brand its rivals are locked out of [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:28:38]. The shared conclusion is a division of labor: the owner keeps the trademark and the marketing engine, and the licensee funds production, inventory and logistics in exchange for borrowed demand.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Seltzer's unit math shows where the money sits. A Star Trek t-shirt retails at Target for $10; the maker spends $3 to produce it, wholesales it for $5, and pays Star Trek a 10% royalty on that $5, or 50 cents. Target takes the biggest cut, but the licensor's 50 cents carries almost no overhead, likely the fattest margin in the chain [qx___lyJ5yQ @ 00:01:50]. Rates move with popularity and the category's margin. Seltzer quotes 8% to 10% as average, Yankees and Major League Baseball at 11% to 12% for t-shirts, Spider-Man and Batman at 12% to 14%, the Olympics at 15% for apparel, Snoopy and Garfield at 8% to 10%, Heathcliff at 6%, and trading cards above 15% because paper carries higher margins [MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:01:35]. On the Brands On Brands podcast the top end climbs, with supply and demand, meaning how many rival bidders show up, driving the spread: the Olympics around 16%, Star Wars and Spider-Man near 16%, food at 5% to 6%, and trading cards closer to 20% [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:12:50]. Daymond John reports the low end: a Walmart supplier earning 6% in electronics may only afford 1%, while the lowest John has really seen is 2% to 3%, with 8% to 12% the normal band [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:05:37].

The second number is the minimum royalty payment guarantee, the floor a licensee owes whether it sells one unit or a million. Seltzer's rule of thumb is to take your own projection and guarantee half: sell $1 million of Batman shirts at a 12% rate, project $120,000 in royalties, guarantee $60,000 [MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:03:44]. That guarantee doubles as the payment schedule: split it into quarters, pay the first $15,000 on signing as the advance, then $15,000 in each of the next three quarters, and multiply the guarantee for two- or three-year terms [MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:04:03]. Daymond John layers it differently: a $5,000 upfront payment plus agreed yearly sales targets, and if year one is set at $10,000 in sales at 10%, the licensee owes $1,000 even if it sells only $5,000 [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:02:37]. Davie Fogarty, whose Oodie has done over $100 million with Disney, Warner Brothers and Nickelodeon licenses, shows how studios hedge against forecasts. Claim $500,000 in sales at 10% and a licensor may set the guarantee at $40,000 against the projected $50,000 royalty, which you still owe if the launch flops or never ships [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:07:09]. Your forecast spreadsheet, which Fogarty says the bigger licensors demand line by line, is the number that gets used against you.

Finding and closing the partner is its own workflow. Fogarty's method is to study a brand you admire that shares your audience, list the licensors it has collaborated with, then hunt adjacent properties; time studio drops to upcoming movie launches, as the Oodie did with Barbie; and work the Las Vegas licensing expo booths for contacts [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:05:24]. Cold outreach follows a script: use the licensor's submission portal if one exists, otherwise message the founder on Instagram or LinkedIn with a mockup showing the overlap of both brands and a stated sales number [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:08:20]. On the Mayer Brown panel, the move for reaching marketing teams is pulling the correspondent from the brand owner's USPTO trademark registration and going straight to that trademark lawyer, or working LinkedIn [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:14:28]. Marcela Dominguez ran the virtual version as an exhibitor: pay for a booth, design it with graphics and video, scour the exhibitor database, send a short blurb on who you are and why you want the meeting, and let accepted contacts book straight into your posted calendar slots [K6BFUviYg0Q @ 00:07:48]. Once talks start, the same panel insists on an NDA first, then a deal memo pre-aligning every point before lawyers draft the long form.

callout.title: Leverage Plays From The Field
callout.body: Four moves operators used to widen margins, open doors at major licensors, and protect launches from ambush.
items: Bundle a marketing levy: FUBU stacked an extra 2% on its 10% royalty across ladies, boots, bags and boys divisions to buy larger spreads in Source, Vibe and Rolling Stone instead of each licensee advertising alone [Daymond John — knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:10:53]

Cold-call the licensing department directly: Stephen Key phoned Disney licensing as a manufacturer, learned no other guitar-pick maker held the category, became a Disney licensee, and later switched to lenticular picks showing 13 frames of a Disney movie [inventRightTV — WMcwXYcUD5c @ 00:02:52]

Niche down to dodge guarantees: smaller licensors contacted in the initial stages often carry very low minimum guarantees or none at all, while Disney and Warner Brothers paperwork makes tiny brands unprofitable for them [Davie Fogarty — 7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:07:39]

Lock domains and socials before any leak: Todd Davitz watched someone buy a campaign domain after a leak and hold the project hostage on a Friday before a Monday execution [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:12:33]

sop_steps.title: Build the licensing strategic plan
sop_steps.action: Map where the brand can be licensed and what each category should earn, then clear marks for those categories and territories.
sop_steps.detail: Seltzer's agency opens outbound engagements with a plan answering which products and categories fit and how much revenue each should return, noting many corporate brands do under $10 million a year in royalty [Brands On Brands Podcast — 3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:15:40]; the Mayer Brown panel adds clearing marks for new applications and geographies and assembling legal, quality control, finance, supply chain, insurance and tax teams [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:11:05].

sop_steps.title: Target and pitch the partner
sop_steps.action: Shortlist licensors from aspirational-brand collaborations and the movie release calendar, then pitch with a mockup and a sales claim.
sop_steps.detail: Use the licensor's portal if one exists, otherwise contact the founder on Instagram or LinkedIn with a mockup of the brand overlap and the number you think you can sell, and get them excited about the collaboration [Davie Fogarty — 7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:08:20].

sop_steps.title: Price the deal on three numbers
sop_steps.action: Set the royalty rate, guarantee half of projected royalties, and schedule the guarantee as four quarterly payments.
sop_steps.detail: Seltzer boils every deal down to the royalty rate, the guaranteed minimum royalty payment, and the payment schedule also known as the advance, then fills in all other terms around them [SeltzerLicensingGrp — MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:00:26].

sop_steps.title: Paper it and run approvals
sop_steps.action: Sign an NDA, align a deal memo, draft the long form, then route every licensed asset through licensor approval.
sop_steps.detail: Get the NDA negotiated first so the business can talk freely, then capture all deal points in a deal memo the lawyers use to build the long-form agreement [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:16:17]; after signing, established licensors open their asset portal and approve every email, product and product image carrying their brand [Davie Fogarty — 7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:09:14].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Rate-setting is the first fault line. Daymond John pegs the working band at 2% up to 15%, with the normal number landing at 8, maybe 10, maybe 12 [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:10:34]. From an 8% to 10% average, Stu Seltzer of SeltzerLicensingGrp charts hot entertainment properties like Spider-Man and Batman at 12 to 14%, the Olympics at 15% for apparel, and a classic like Heathcliff the cat at 6% [MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:01:54]. On the Brands On Brands Podcast, Seltzer stretches both ends of the range: food products with slimmer margins sit closer to 5% or 6%, and paper products like trading cards can run closer to 20% because those margins are even higher [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:13:09]. The fashion-licensing channel Patents, Trademarks & Business Protection frames the spread as commonly between 3% and 15% of sales [tHEEzY7Mwgc @ 00:01:58]. The operator read is that no single number is standard. Seltzer names the two inputs that move it: brand heat, driven by supply and demand and how many manufacturers are bidding, and what the licensee's category margin can actually carry. A 5% food deal and a 20% trading-card deal can both be rational under the same playbook. Price the brand to the category, not to the ego.

The minimum guarantee splits practitioners on how hard the floor should bite. Seltzer's rule of thumb is mechanical: project year-one sales, multiply by the rate, and guarantee half, so $1 million of Batman tees at 12% projects $120,000 in royalties and a $60,000 guarantee [MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:03:44]. Davie Fogarty describes a licensor taking a $500,000 sales projection and $50,000 projected royalty and setting the guarantee at $40,000 to hedge its bets, far above Seltzer's 50% line [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:07:09]. Daymond John strips the math down: 10% of gross, a $5,000 upfront payment, and a year-one floor where a $10,000 target means $1,000 owed no matter what [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:02:37]. The royalty base is contested too. Daymond quotes gross sales, while the Mayer Brown panel lays out net sales, a percentage of the MSRP of a component product such as a computer chip inside a computer, and tiered structures where the rate decreases once sales milestones are reached [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:20:47]. For the operator, the guarantee is the real price of the license: the rate only costs money when product sells, the floor costs money when it does not. Negotiate the base and the floor before haggling over a point of rate.

Access strategy is the sharpest split. Fogarty warns that Disney and Warner Brothers carry so much legal paperwork they will not profit from a really small brand, so the move is to niche down [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:06:37]. Stephen Key of inventRightTV lived the opposite: Key cold-called the Disney licensing department as a guitar-pick maker, was asked how long the company had been in business and how many stores carried it, answered a couple of years and a couple thousand, and was offered the open guitar-pick category [WMcwXYcUD5c @ 00:03:29]. Seltzer adds a third path through an agency, landing first-ever NFL rights for Sterling Sports, an inflatables maker under $25 million that took a blow-up recliner to QVC and almost tripled company sales [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:09:53]. Marcela Dominguez of TrademarkLawyer ran the do-it-yourself route as a licensor, exhibiting the Stowy Joey brand at a virtual Licensing Expo and booking meetings by sending a quick blurb on who you are and why you want the meeting [K6BFUviYg0Q @ 00:07:48]. The contrast comes down to leverage: niche licensors trade prestige for soft guarantees, majors screen on operating history and store count, and agents sell access a founder cannot open alone.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is the guarantee you cannot hit. Seltzer spells out the downside: a licensee that projected 200,000 Star Trek tees but sold one, or hit some hitch where nobody wanted to buy, is suddenly on the hook for the full $50,000 guarantee [qx___lyJ5yQ @ 00:04:47]. Fogarty puts it bluntly for small e-commerce brands: fail to launch or fail to sell what you forecast and you still owe the money, even if no product ever ships because the launch did not work out [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:07:24]. The inverse failure hit Fogarty's first Warner Brothers launch built on Friends and Harry Potter assets, run while still living at home with parents: over $500,000 in just a few weeks, completely sold out, and by Fogarty's own account it could have been a lot bigger with real inventory management [7U8vYps8fMk @ 00:01:35]. Upside stockouts and downside guarantees are the same disease: a forecast nobody pressure-tested. Seltzer closes the loop on the Brands On Brands Podcast, naming financial risk, inventory risk, and brand risk for a brand owner as exposures every operator must analyze before entering a deal [3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:29:57]. Size the floor off a forecast your own team believes, then build stock against the upside case.

Before signing, run Daymond John's value test. If a licensee already moves 1,000 pairs of $100 jeans a month and a 15% license neither lifts price to $115 nor lifts volume toward 10,000 pairs, the brand has simply become a $15 charge on the same units [knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:08:34]. Seltzer's Star Trek breakdown keeps egos in check: on a $10 Target tee costing $3 to make and wholesaling at $5, the retailer makes most of the money, the manufacturer earns a decent margin, and the brand takes 50 cents on very little overhead [qx___lyJ5yQ @ 00:01:50]. Scope drafting is the next landmine. A Mayer Brown presenter involved in the Corona dispute recounts that Constellation's license covered beer, defined largely along regulatory lines, hard seltzers did not exist at signing, and Constellation won the lawsuit and the appeal to sell seltzer [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:58:54]. The panel warns that a mark used beyond its defined goods can breach other license agreements, invite third-party claims, and sour an otherwise lucrative partnership [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:24:08]. The fix taught is an explicit product schedule that specifically excludes anything not identified, plus a deliberate look ahead at categories that do not exist yet. Draft for the product that has not been invented.

Execution failures are often self-inflicted. Mayer Brown's Todd Davitz describes a funded execution where a leak let someone buy the domain name and hold the whole project hostage, surfacing on a Friday with a Monday go-live, so domain names and NDAs get locked first; a co-presenter adds socials and any name, image and likeness rights to the same list [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:12:33]. On another deal, marketing swore it needed only a fixed set of TV spot lengths, then needed an extra 45-second and a six-second spot the agreement never covered, and only the goodwill from being nice to the other side bought the flexibility [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:18:18]. AI adds fresh exposure: the panel warns that a jingle spat out by an AI music studio is not something you will own, so ownable campaign assets need deliberate human authorship [yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:49:52]. On the licensor side, Marcela Dominguez of TrademarkLawyer warns that a partner who misrepresents your brand, mission, or values can taint it so badly that nobody else wants to work with you, so due diligence happens before you sign anything, not after [ASLTB9jyYII @ 00:04:45]. Every one of these losses was cheap to prevent at the term sheet and expensive to fix after launch.

callout.title: Pre-Signature Kill Switch
callout.body: Do not sign or launch until every check below clears, because each one maps to a loss a practitioner took or watched happen.
items: Cap the minimum guarantee at half of your own year-one royalty projection and push back on licensor floors like a $40,000 hedge on a $50,000 projection [SeltzerLicensingGrp — MGH55iIT-A0 @ 00:03:25].
Prove the license lifts price or volume, using the $100-to-$115 jeans test, or the royalty is pure cost on the same units [Daymond John — knoob7eUS6Y @ 00:08:34].
Secure domain names, socials, and NDAs before deal chatter leaks, or risk a launch held hostage over a weekend [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:12:33].
Write a licensed-products definition that specifically excludes anything not identified, so a hard-seltzer-style scope fight cannot reach court [Mayer Brown — yRNAVrfCNIE @ 00:23:23].

chapters.pull_quote: "When fans love your brand, they will buy other products and services with that brand on it." — Stu Seltzer, Brands On Brands Podcast (3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:19:43).
action_checklist: Run the brand-readiness test: how many people know the brand, whether they know what it stands for, and whether consumers give it permission to extend [Brands On Brands Podcast — 3tCB_MAOXkA @ 00:20:34].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I evaluate a patent portfolio and choose among licensing, brokered sales and NPE monetization?
chapters.title: Value and Monetize Patent Portfolios
chapters.subtitle: IP holding companies, unused assets, valuation, monetization costs, portfolio readiness, patent brokers, seller motivations, NPEs, Fractus, Arm and Qualcomm
chapters.executive_summary: Operators who buy, broker, fund, and assert patents converge on one rule: a patent with no evidence of use and no enforcement threat does not sell and does not license. Funders pass on 19 of every 20 portfolios, brokers accept one or two percent of intake, and money flows to claim-charted, multi-family portfolios backing cases with at least $100M in damages. The street numbers are blunt. US litigation runs $12-20M at full rates. The starting proceeds split is 50/30/20 between owner, funder, and law firm. Broker commissions run 10-30%, and sales take 6-18 months. Qualcomm's 3-5% per-phone royalty and Arm's $2.61B royalty line show the upside. Practitioners split on whether NPEs are essential leverage or a value-draining middleman, and on whether a falling buyer's market still rewards selling over licensing.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who touches money in this market starts from the same premise: a patent is worth what its owner can credibly enforce. Fractus co-founder Carles Puente pivoted from manufacturing millions of antennas to research and licensing. Puente puts it flatly: without enforcing the rights, patents have no value. For Fractus as an SME, that enforcement had to happen in the US, and it was painful and difficult [fAwWxzitmUk @ 00:03:48]. Silicon Valley Business School host David Smith is even blunter: companies usually do not pay patent licenses until they are forced to, so licensing is driven by litigation [hOFtwRua-qc @ 00:05:16]. The Transpacific IP guest on IPWatchdog describes the same reality from the owner side. Their firm runs carrot licensing, but the carrot only works when backed by a heavy stick [qZqv5lEPPQc @ 00:00:25]. Louis Carbonneau of Tangible IP has brokered more than 4,500 patents, and they turn this into a sales law: if there is no evidence that anyone is practicing the patents, they can predict with 100% certainty that the portfolio will not sell [t98CwzofUz0 @ 00:34:27]. The operator takeaway is that the asset is evidence of use plus a believable enforcement path. The certificate itself is just paperwork.

The second point of agreement is that the overwhelming majority of granted patents are dead inventory. Berkeley Law & Technology Group cites the figure that roughly 90% of patents never generate revenue, because inventors patent ideas and never commercialize them [oRUwDt8nD5k @ 00:00:00]. Anders Arison of Parallel North IP, a former head of patent acquisitions at Nokia, narrows it further. Over 1 million patents are granted every year, yet only about 5% are monetized, held back by gaps in awareness, funding, and expertise [_bueYwQ3iHE @ 00:10:00]. Silicon Valley Business School frames the same waste as a placement problem: so many patents sit unused because they are essentially in the wrong hands, while the channels to market are held by a few large corporations [vPziFABPW9w @ 00:01:35]. The people who actually write checks confirm how narrow the funnel is. The IPWatchdog funding panel reports that funders pass on 19 of every 20 portfolios. They check damages, venue, marking, prior licenses, grant interests, and market size before they ever look at technical merits [pyi_x9MFGjs @ 00:23:42]. For an operator, the default outcome for any portfolio is rejection. The job is to prove the asset belongs in the small slice that actually moves.

Practitioners also agree that a single patent rarely carries a campaign. Depth, coverage, and honest internal triage come first. The funding panel moderated by Brad Close warns that one newly issued patent means a portfolio is not ready. The panel urges owners to file multiple families and aim for three to six independent assets [pyi_x9MFGjs @ 00:32:09]. The host of the Transpacific IP conversation goes further, estimating that a portfolio of 10 good patents requires at least 100. The guest adds that a few patents only work in support of an operating company [qZqv5lEPPQc @ 00:25:01]. Inside an operating company, Dean Keebler of Samtec runs every patent through three tests. Does it cover our product or a competitor's? Will it survive litigation? Will a third party think it survives? If not, Keebler questions its value [1UEOTCZ_qYA @ 00:04:56]. Useless Money adds the commercial filter that separates paper from cash flow: legal protection and commercial demand are two different things, and no universal royalty rate applies to every patent, brand, or software product [xkXjle5Spjw @ 00:05:23]. The baseline prerequisite is a portfolio deep enough to survive invalidity attacks and mapped to real products before anyone spends a dollar on outreach.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The cost of an enforcement campaign is where most owners get sticker shock. On the IPWatchdog economics panel moderated by Brad Close, a US case at full rates runs $12-20M. Litigation finance is non-recourse, so investors lose their capital on a loss. Firms defer 40-50% of their fees, which drops a $12M case to about $6M, while the funder still covers $2-3M in hard costs [pyi_x9MFGjs @ 00:05:41]. The same panel's starting split is 50% to the patent owner, 30% to the funder, and 20% to the law firm, and funding is reserved for damages of at least $100M. Louis Carbonneau prices a suit against Samsung or Apple at $3-5M and says plaintiffs win roughly one in three or one in four times, so plaintiffs must choose cases very selectively [t98CwzofUz0 @ 00:56:03]. Defending the asset costs real money too. The Transpacific IP conversation puts a PTAB defense at $300K to about $1M [qZqv5lEPPQc @ 00:46:07]. David Smith prices an IPR at about $250,000 and expert time at $356-478 per hour, based on more than 35,000 cases [hOFtwRua-qc @ 00:07:16]. The operator math is simple: unless the damages pool dwarfs a multi-million-dollar spend, no funder or contingency firm will carry the case.

Selling or brokering runs on its own price list and calendar. UpCounsel reports that most brokers work on a commission of 10 to 30% of the sale price, and that most transactions take 6 to 18 months. The deal moves from a sales package to redacted outreach to a purchase agreement with independent legal review [xRRc9i7j5A8 @ 00:04:11]. Anders Arison quantifies the glut. Asking prices total about $44B against roughly $12-13B actually sold. Brokers represented about 70% of patents and 87% of packages, and it is now a buyer's market with falling prices [_bueYwQ3iHE @ 00:16:24]. Louis Carbonneau's vetting order mirrors a funder's: assertion potential using litigation-grade claim charts, then validity including priority and section 101, then likely targets, then damages. The blunt rule is that $1 million in damages against $5 million to litigate does not sell [t98CwzofUz0 @ 00:35:13]. J.D. Houvener, who claims about 500 patents over 10 years, says hiring a broker is better if you can afford it. A broker takes the emotionally invested inventor out of the talks, and buyers lower their guard with a professional across the table [a7AlJrwA2Jo @ 00:01:15]. Price, timing, and representation are set in the broker agreement before the first buyer call. UpCounsel says that agreement covers exclusivity, compensation, and duration.

The royalty structures that pay at scale are surprisingly simple. The Strategy Breakdown reports that Qualcomm collects 3 to 5% of the wholesale price of nearly every phone. Qualcomm refuses pass-through: chipmakers license the IP just to build the chip, and OEMs pay a separate device-level royalty on the full wholesale price. Its licensing arm, QTL, is about 20% of revenue but 60% of profits [uNc4jO7TeCo @ 00:05:14]. Kingacademic UK describes Arm's two-layer model: an upfront license fee opens access, and a royalty is paid on each shipped product. In FY2026 that produced royalty revenue of $2.61B, up 21%, and license and other revenue of $2.31B, up 25% [aRUsXPICxpY @ 00:01:23]. Useless Money breaks down InterDigital: about $834M of 2025 revenue and $461M of operating income. A July 2025 Samsung arbitration result of $1.05B covers January 2023 to December 2030, which the company equated to roughly $131M in recurring revenue per year [xkXjle5Spjw @ 00:06:53]. For inventors feeding an NPE, David Smith insists on gross revenue-sharing over profit-sharing, because it is difficult to argue about the definition of revenue. Smith cites a case where $1M was billed for photocopies. Under an 80/20 split, a $1M license pays the inventor $200,000 [hOFtwRua-qc @ 00:18:09]. Lock down the royalty base before negotiating anything else.
